title: Who cares for the young? Sexual selection, family systems and fathers who carry the eggs

summary.text: On a lotus pond in India, the bird sitting on the eggs is the father, and a seahorse father carries the eggs in a pouch. Who looks after the young, and why? In this lesson you will guess first, run the Warm Egg Test with steel tumblers of warm water, and play a game.
summary.art: A lotus pond with a small bronze-winged jacana father sitting on a floating nest, a larger female jacana walking on the leaves nearby, and a child with a notebook watching from the bank.

intro.hook: A seahorse mother places her eggs in a pouch on the father's belly. He carries them for weeks, and then he gives birth. On Indian ponds, a jacana father sits on the eggs alone. Why does the father do the caring in some animals, and the mother in others?
intro.text: Animals raise their young in many ways. Two pigeons share one nest and take turns. One male elephant seal lives with dozens of females and looks after no pups at all. A turtle mother buries her eggs and never sees them hatch. In this lesson you first guess who looks after the young in eight animal families. Then you test, with warm water in steel tumblers, what an egg needs from the ones who sit on it. The result explains a lot about bird families. After that you meet the idea that explains the rest. It is called sexual selection.
intro.art: A pregnant-looking seahorse father holding a blade of seagrass with his tail, with a few tiny young seahorses drifting out of the pouch on his belly.

outcomes: I can say what makes an animal female or male: the size of the sex cells they make.
I can explain sexual selection and its two parts, which are competing for partners and choosing partners.
I can name five family systems in nature and give an animal for each.
I can explain why the parent who gives more to each young is usually the choosier one, and what happens when the roles swap.
I can use my Warm Egg Test results to explain why most birds raise young as a pair and most mammals do not.
I can describe how a seahorse father carries the young, and name other fathers who do the caring.
I can describe animal groups that females lead, and say what the leader does for the group.
I can tell what was seen from what was guessed, and say why what other animals do is not a rule for people.

terms.meaning: A special cell that carries half of the instructions for building a new animal. Two sex cells must join to start a new life.
terms.example: An egg cell and a sperm are both sex cells.
terms.art: A large round cell and a tiny cell with a tail drawn side by side, with a child's finger pointing at each.

terms.meaning: The larger kind of sex cell. Egg cells carry food for the first days of the new life.
terms.example: A human egg cell is about a tenth of a millimetre wide, like a tiny dot of pencil.
terms.art: A round egg cell drawn large, with a pencil dot beside it to show the real size.

terms.meaning: The smaller kind of sex cell. Sperm carry almost no food, and most kinds can swim.
terms.example: A sperm's head is about twenty times narrower than an egg cell.
terms.art: Many tiny cells with tails swimming towards one large round egg cell.

terms.meaning: A female is an animal who makes the larger sex cells, the egg cells. A male is an animal who makes the smaller ones, the sperm.
terms.example: A seahorse father is male because he makes sperm, even though he carries the young.
terms.art: A hen and a rooster side by side, with a large egg cell drawn above her and tiny sperm drawn above him.

terms.meaning: The joining of one egg cell and one sperm. The joined cell can grow into a new animal.
terms.example: A frog's eggs are fertilised in the pond water, outside the mother's body.
terms.art: One small cell with a tail touching a large round cell, with an arrow to a ball of a few cells.

terms.meaning: The way some animals have more young than others because they do better at winning partners. Over many generations it shapes bodies and behaviour.
terms.example: A blackbuck's long twisted horns came from sexual selection.
terms.art: Two male blackbuck with long spiral horns locked together on a dry grassland, with females grazing behind.

terms.meaning: One part of sexual selection. Animals of one sex fight or outdo each other to get partners.
terms.example: Two male elephant seals rear up and slam their chests together on a beach.
terms.art: Two huge male elephant seals rearing up chest to chest on a beach, with smaller females lying around.

terms.meaning: The other part of sexual selection. An animal watches or listens, compares, and accepts or refuses a partner.
terms.example: A peahen walks past several peacocks before she accepts one.
terms.art: A peahen walking past three displaying peacocks, looking at each in turn.

terms.meaning: Anything a parent does after eggs are laid or young are born that helps the young to live.
terms.example: A pigeon sitting on eggs and feeding the chicks is giving parental care.
terms.art: A pigeon on a ledge nest bending down to feed a small chick.

terms.meaning: Everything a parent spends on one young: the food in the egg, the time, the energy and the risk. What is spent on one young cannot be spent on another.
terms.example: An emperor penguin father goes without food for about four months to hatch one egg.
terms.art: An emperor penguin father standing in snow with one egg resting on his feet under a fold of belly skin.

terms.meaning: Keeping eggs warm until they hatch, usually by sitting on them.
terms.example: Pigeon parents take turns to incubate two eggs for about 18 days.
terms.art: A pigeon sitting low on a nest with the edge of a white egg just showing under her feathers.

terms.meaning: A family system in which one female and one male stay together for at least one breeding season.
terms.example: Two sarus cranes hold a patch of wetland together and both sit on the eggs.
terms.art: Two tall grey sarus cranes with red heads standing beside a nest mound in a flooded paddy field.

terms.meaning: A family system in which one male has several female partners at the same time.
terms.example: One silverback gorilla lives with several females and their young.
terms.art: A large silverback gorilla sitting with three smaller females and two infants in a forest clearing.

terms.meaning: A group of several females who share one male partner, or of several males who share one female partner.
terms.example: A male elephant seal guards a harem of dozens of females on a beach.
terms.art: A beach with one very large seal in the middle of a tight group of many smaller seals.

terms.meaning: A family system in which one female has several male partners at the same time.
terms.example: A female bronze-winged jacana may have up to four mates, and each sits on a clutch of her eggs.
terms.art: One large jacana on lotus leaves with three smaller jacanas, each sitting on his own floating nest.

terms.meaning: A family system in which both females and males have several partners and no lasting pair forms.
terms.example: Chimpanzees live in big groups where females and males each have several partners.
terms.art: A group of chimpanzees of mixed ages sitting and grooming each other in a forest.

terms.meaning: A family system in which helpers who are not the parents also feed, carry or guard the young.
terms.example: In an elephant family, aunts and older sisters watch over a calf.
terms.art: A small elephant calf walking between her mother and two other adult females who shade her with their bodies.

terms.meaning: The female who leads a group. She is often the oldest.
terms.example: An elephant matriarch leads her family to water she remembers from years ago.
terms.art: An old female elephant walking at the front of a line of females and calves across dry ground.

terms.meaning: A pocket of skin in which a parent carries eggs or young. In seahorses the pouch is on the father.
terms.example: A seahorse father's brood pouch gives the growing young oxygen and some food.
terms.art: A cut-away drawing of a seahorse father's belly pouch with tiny young curled inside.

terms.meaning: A family system in which the females compete for partners and the males do the caring. It is the reverse of the more common pattern.
terms.example: Female jacanas fight each other over patches of pond, and the males raise the chicks.
terms.art: Two large female jacanas facing each other with wings raised on lotus leaves, while a smaller male sits on a nest behind.

terms.meaning: An animal who makes both egg cells and sperm, either at the same time or at different times in life.
terms.example: An earthworm makes both egg cells and sperm.
terms.art: Two earthworms lying side by side on wet soil.

explanations.concept: What female and male mean: two sizes of sex cell
explanations.definition: A female is an animal who makes the larger sex cells, called egg cells. A male is an animal who makes the smaller sex cells, called sperm.
explanations.description: A new animal usually starts when two sex cells join. Each sex cell carries half of the instructions, which are written in a long molecule called DNA. In almost all animals the two sex cells are very different in size. Egg cells are large, because they also carry food and the working parts of a cell. Sperm are tiny, and carry little more than their half of the instructions. A human egg cell is about a tenth of a millimetre wide, so you could just see one as a dot. The head of a human sperm is about twenty times narrower. This difference in size is the only thing that makes an animal female or male, in every kind of animal. Colour is not what makes an animal female or male. Neither is size, strength or caring. A seahorse father carries the young, and he is male because he makes sperm. But why would the difference in sex cells matter for families? Because large cells cost more to make. A female's body can make only a limited number of egg cells. A male's body can make a very large number of sperm. The other explanations follow from that one fact.
examples: A hen's yolk is one giant egg cell, packed with food. A rooster's sperm are far too small to see.
A female jacana is bigger and fiercer than her mates. She is still the female, because she makes the egg cells.
The tiny power stations inside your cells, called mitochondria, almost always come from the egg cell, so from your mother.
explanations.art: A large round egg cell with one tiny sperm touching the edge, and a ruler mark showing a tenth of a millimetre.

explanations.concept: Why are there two sizes at all?
explanations.description: Nobody watched the two sizes of sex cell first appear, because it happened long before there were any animals, in living beings made of one cell or a few cells. Scientists think the first sex cells were all one size. Some pond algae alive today still make sex cells of one size, so they have no females and no males. In 1972 Geoff Parker, Robin Baker and Vic Smith worked out with maths how two sizes could arise. A parent has a fixed amount of material to make sex cells from. A parent can make a few large cells or many small ones. Two large cells that join make a well-fed start, which is more likely to live. Many small cells find partners more often, simply because there are more of them. A middle size does badly both ways, because such cells are too few to find partners and too small to feed the young. So over many generations the middle disappears and two kinds are left. This is the leading idea, and it fits what we see in algae. It has not been proved.
examples: Some green pond algae have sex cells of one size. Their close relatives have large and small ones.
Think of sharing one lump of dough. You can make three big balls or thirty tiny ones, but not thirty big ones.

perspectives.who: Geoff Parker, Robin Baker and Vic Smith, 1972
perspectives.explanation: Two sizes win because many small cells find more partners and large cells feed the young. Middle-sized cells lose on both counts.
Other causes may matter too, such as how easily sex cells meet in open water. The question is still being worked on.

explanations.art: One lump of dough on the left, and on the right the same amount shaped as three big balls on one plate and thirty tiny balls on another.

explanations.definition: Sexual selection is the way some animals leave more young than others because they are better at winning partners. It has two parts: competing with rivals of your own sex, and being chosen by the other sex.
explanations.description: Charles Darwin described sexual selection in his book The Descent of Man in 1871. He was puzzled by features that do not help an animal to find food or to stay safe. A blackbuck's horns are long and twisted, and only the males usually have them. A peacock's train makes him easy for a tiger to see. Darwin's answer was that these features help their owner to have young. This happens in two ways. The first is competition. Animals of one sex fight or threaten each other, and the winners get more partners. Horns, tusks and big bodies come from this. The second is choice. Animals of the other sex compare and pick, and the ones who are picked have more young. Trains, songs and dances come from this. A feature that wins more partners is passed on to more young, so it spreads, even if it makes life harder in other ways. Both parts can act on one animal. A male blackbuck fights for a small patch of ground, and then females choose among the patches.
examples: Chital stags grow antlers and push against each other with them. The does have no antlers.
Male Asian elephants push and chase each other for the chance to mate, and the larger male usually wins.
Female jacanas compete with each other for mates, so competition is not only something males do.
explanations.art: A split picture: on the left two male blackbuck with horns locked, on the right a female blackbuck walking between several males who each stand on a small patch of bare ground.

explanations.concept: Parental investment: whoever gives more to each young chooses more carefully
explanations.definition: Parental investment is everything a parent spends on one young, including the food in the egg, the time, the energy and the risk. The sex that spends more on each young is usually the choosier one. The other sex usually competes.
explanations.description: In 1972 Robert Trivers asked why males are usually the ones who compete and females the ones who choose. His answer was about cost. Think of a cow and a bull. The cow carries a calf for nine months and then feeds the calf milk for months. She can have about one calf a year, whoever her partner is. A poor choice of partner costs her a whole year. The bull spends very little on each calf, so a poor choice costs him almost nothing. That is why she is careful. There is a second reason. While the cow is busy with a calf, she is not looking for a partner. So at any moment many bulls are ready to breed and few cows are. The bulls must compete for the few cows who are ready. Trivers's idea makes a prediction that can be tested. If the father of some species spends more than the mother, the roles should swap. They do. Jacana fathers do all the sitting and chick care, and jacana females are the ones who fight. A male Mormon cricket gives the female a large packet of food when they mate. Darryl Gwynne found in 1981 that these males refuse most females, and the females compete for the males.
examples: A male giant water bug carries the eggs glued to his back until they hatch. While he carries them he cannot mate again, and females seek out males who are free.
A female elephant seal fasts for about 23 days while she feeds her pup. The father gives the pup nothing.
A pigeon mother and father spend about the same on each chick, and they look alike and court each other.
explanations.art: A balance with a cow and her calf on one pan and a bull on the other, with the cow's side much heavier and labelled 'nine months and milk'.

explanations.concept: Every young has one mother and one father
explanations.definition: In animals with two sexes, each young has exactly one mother and one father. So all the females together have the same number of young as all the males together.
explanations.description: This sounds too obvious to matter, but it corrects a common mistake. People often say that males can have far more young than females. One male can. All males cannot. Suppose a beach has 10 male and 10 female seals, and 10 pups are born. The females have 10 pups between them, about one each. The males also have 10 pups between them, because every pup has a father. If one big male fathers 8 of the pups, the other nine males share only 2. Most of them father none. So the average is the same for both sexes, and what differs is how evenly the young are shared out. Among the females, nearly every one has a pup. Among the males, a few have many and most have none. That uneven sharing is why the males fight so hard. A male who loses has no young at all. Scientists call this rule the Fisher condition, after Ronald Fisher, who used it in 1930.
examples: In elephant seals a few large males father most of the pups on a beach, and many males never father any.
In pigeons, who live as pairs, nearly every female and nearly every male raises chicks, so there is little to fight over.
explanations.art: Ten seal pups in a row, each joined by one line to a mother and one line to a father. The mothers' lines are spread evenly. Eight of the fathers' lines go to one large male.

explanations.definition: A family system, which scientists call a mating system, is the usual pattern of who pairs with whom in a species, and for how long.
explanations.description: Scientists use five main names. In monogamy, one female and one male stay together for a season or longer. Sarus cranes, pigeons and hoolock gibbons live this way. In polygyny, one male has several female partners. A group of females with one male is called a harem. Gorillas and elephant seals live this way. In polyandry, one female has several male partners. Jacanas live this way. In promiscuity, females and males each have several partners and no pair lasts. Chimpanzees live this way. In cooperative breeding, helpers who are not the parents also raise the young. Elephants do this, and so do people. These names describe what animals are seen doing. They are not grades from good to bad, and no system is more advanced than another. One species can also use more than one system, depending on where the animals live and how many partners are about.
examples: Pair: two great hornbills raise one or two chicks in a tree hollow in the Western Ghats.
One male, several females: a silverback gorilla with his group.
One female, several males: a bronze-winged jacana on a lotus pond.
Helpers: older sisters and aunts in an elephant family.
explanations.art: Five small panels in a row: two cranes, a gorilla with three females, a large jacana with three small ones, a group of chimpanzees, and an elephant calf among several adult females.

explanations.concept: A pair you can see is not always the whole story
explanations.definition: A social pair is two animals who live together and raise young together. It does not always mean that every chick in the nest has that male as the father.
explanations.description: Until the 1980s, scientists could only watch who lived with whom. Most birds live in pairs, so most birds were called faithful. Then a way was found to read DNA and work out who a chick's real parents are. The surprise was large. In 2002 Simon Griffith, Ian Owens and Katherine Thuman put together more than 150 such studies. In about nine out of ten kinds of birds tested, some chicks had a father who was not the male at the nest. In birds that live as pairs, about 11 chicks in every 100 had another father. So the pair is real. The two birds do build the nest and feed the chicks together. But who lives together and who the parents are turn out to be two separate questions. This is also a lesson about evidence. What we see from outside is a start, and a new tool can show what watching alone missed.
examples: A pair of pigeons usually stays together for years, but matings outside the pair do happen.
A female bird may live with one male and still have a chick fathered by a neighbour.
explanations.art: A bird's nest with four chicks, three coloured like the male perched beside the nest and one coloured like a different male on a far branch.

explanations.concept: Why most birds are pairs and most mammals are not
explanations.definition: In about four out of five kinds of birds, both parents care for the young. In mammals, fathers help with the young in only about one kind in ten or fewer.
explanations.description: The difference comes from what the young need and who is able to give it. A bird's egg must be kept warm almost all the time, close to the warmth of the parent's body. A mother or a father can do this equally well. But a bird who sits cannot look for food. If one parent sits alone, the eggs cool each time that parent leaves to eat. You measure this cooling in the Warm Egg Test. With two parents, one sits while the other feeds. After hatching, many chicks need food brought many times an hour, and two parents can bring about twice as much. So a bird father who stays usually raises far more chicks than one who leaves. A baby mammal grows inside the mother, which keeps the baby warm with no sitting. After birth the baby needs milk, and only the mother makes milk. There is much less a father can add, so in most mammals he gains more by seeking other partners. About 9 in 100 kinds of mammals live as pairs. Where mammal fathers do help, they carry, guard or feed the young, as in wolves and some monkeys.
examples: A great hornbill mother seals herself inside a tree hollow, leaving only a slit. The father passes food to her and the chicks through the slit for weeks.
Both pigeon parents make a rich food called crop milk in a pouch in the throat, so both can feed the newly hatched chicks.
A newborn calf drinks only milk, so only the mother can feed her.
explanations.art: On the left a hornbill father passing a fig through a slit in a sealed tree hollow. On the right a cow feeding a calf while the bull grazes far away.

explanations.concept: The seahorse: a father who carries the young
explanations.definition: In seahorses the female places her eggs in a brood pouch on the male's belly. He fertilises them there, carries them until they hatch, and gives birth to live young.
explanations.description: A pair of seahorses greet each other soon after dawn each day. They swim side by side and brighten in colour. When the female's eggs are ready, the two rise through the water together. She puts a tube into the opening of his pouch and passes the eggs in. In one species that was studied, the pouch stays open for only about six seconds. The eggs are fertilised inside the pouch. Then the pouch closes. For the next 9 to 45 days, depending on the kind of seahorse, the father's body does much of what a mammal mother's body does. The lining of the pouch brings oxygen to the young and carries their waste away. It gives them some fat and calcium. It also keeps the liquid around them at the right saltiness. Then the father squeezes his body, usually at night, and pushes out the young, usually 100 to 1,000 of them. They get no care after that, and fewer than 1 in 200 lives to grow up. The father is often ready for new eggs by the next morning.
examples: Seahorses live in seagrass beds and river mouths along the coasts of India.
Pipefish are relatives of seahorses. Pipefish fathers also carry the eggs.
The seahorse mother's eggs cost her a great deal. Making one batch can use up about a third of her body weight.
explanations.art: Two seahorses rising belly to belly through green seagrass, the female passing eggs into the open pouch of the male.

explanations.concept: Why seahorse fathers, and not mothers?
explanations.description: Nobody knows for certain why the carrying fell to the father in seahorses. Several ideas have been offered, and none has been proved. One idea is about speed. While the father carries one batch, the mother's body is already making the next batch of eggs. The two jobs run at the same time, so the pair can produce young faster than if one parent did both jobs in turn. A second idea is about certainty. The eggs are fertilised inside his own pouch, so the father can be sure the young are his. Care is less wasted when a parent is sure. A third idea starts earlier in history. In many fish the male already guards a patch of sea floor where eggs are laid. Guarding eggs on your patch, then on your skin, then in a fold of skin, are small steps, and pipefish alive today show each of them. Here is a surprise that tests your thinking. Seahorse males still compete more than females do, by wrestling with their tails. Carrying the young did not swap every role.
examples: Some pipefish fathers carry eggs stuck to the outside of the belly. Others have skin flaps over them. Seahorses have a closed pouch.
Male seahorses snap their heads at rivals and wrestle with their tails.

perspectives.explanation: Father carries while mother makes the next eggs, so the pair has more young in a season.
Fertilising the eggs inside his own pouch makes the father sure that the young are his.
Male fish already guarded eggs on their patch. A pouch is the far end of a long row of small changes.

explanations.art: Three related fish in a row: a pipefish with eggs stuck under the belly, a pipefish with skin flaps half covering the eggs, and a seahorse with a closed round pouch.

explanations.concept: Fish and frogs: when the eggs are outside, the father often guards
explanations.description: Most fish give their eggs no care at all. But in about 3 fish families out of 10, some kinds do care. When one parent cares alone, that parent is the father more often than the mother. This is the reverse of mammals. Why? In most fish the eggs are fertilised in the water, outside the mother's body. A male fish often holds a patch of the bottom and waits for females to lay there. He is already guarding that patch against rivals. Guarding the eggs that lie on it costs him little extra. He can also guard the eggs of several females at once. Meanwhile the female can go and feed, and make more eggs. This is the explanation most scientists favour today, but it is not settled. A clownfish father fans the eggs with his fins and picks out the dead ones for six to eight days.
examples: A clownfish father guards and fans the eggs beside the sea anemone where the pair lives.
Sardines and many other sea fish release their eggs into open water and give them no care.

perspectives.who: The patch idea, favoured by most scientists
perspectives.explanation: A male who already defends a patch to attract females can guard eggs on it at little extra cost.
When eggs are fertilised outside the body in front of him, a male is surer that they are his.

explanations.art: An orange and white clownfish fanning a patch of small orange eggs on a rock beside a sea anemone.

explanations.concept: The jacana: a test that the theory passed
explanations.definition: In jacanas the usual roles are reversed. The female holds a territory with one to four males in it. Each male incubates a clutch of her eggs and raises the chicks alone.
explanations.description: The bronze-winged jacana walks on lotus and water lily leaves on ponds across India, on very long toes. The female is much heavier than the male. In one sample from southern India, females weighed about 282 grams and males about 176 grams. She defends a stretch of pond against other females. Inside it, each of her mates has a smaller patch. She lays four eggs for one male, and he sits on them for about 29 days. Then she lays for the next male. When danger comes, a father tucks the chicks between his wings and his body and carries them off. Why did this family system arise? Scientists think one part of the answer is that a female who is free of sitting can quickly lay a new clutch, for the same male or another, when a nest is lost. How often jacana nests are lost to floods and egg-eaters has not been well measured, so this is an idea, not a settled fact. Stuart Butchart and his team found something more in 1999. The males in a harem compete too, by calling loudly to bring the female to them. Males who called more got more matings. So even here, both competing and choosing go on.
examples: A female pheasant-tailed jacana may lay up to ten clutches in one season, each for a different male to raise.
Female jacanas chase and fight other females who come into their stretch of pond.
The male, who spends the most on each chick, is the one the females compete for. Trivers's idea predicted this.
explanations.art: A small jacana father standing on a lotus leaf with two pairs of long chick legs dangling from under his wings.

explanations.definition: One animal can keep several partners only where those partners, or the things they need, are gathered closely enough to be guarded.
explanations.description: Why do elephant seals have harems when pigeons do not? In 1977 Stephen Emlen and Lewis Oring gave an answer that you can test on a table with coins. Female seals must come ashore to give birth, and good beaches are few. So the females crowd together. One strong male can stand in the middle and keep other males away from dozens of females. Female pigeons are spread over a whole city, each at a nest. No male could guard several. A male pigeon does better by staying at one nest and helping. So the family system depends partly on where the females are and how closely they gather. Kavita Isvaran of the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru studied blackbuck in this way. She found that where female blackbuck move in large groups, males gather on small patches packed close together. Such a gathering is called a lek. Females visit the lek and choose among the males. Where females are few and scattered, males hold larger patches far apart.
examples: In the One Guard Test, you find out how many coins one hand can guard when they are close together, and when they are spread out.
A male elephant seal weighs more than three tonnes. Only the biggest males can hold the middle of the beach.
Sarus crane pairs hold a large patch of wetland. One male could not guard two such patches.
explanations.art: A beach seen from above with females crowded into one small cove and one large male beside them, and beside it a city map with pigeon nests dotted far apart.

explanations.definition: In some animals the group is built around related females, and a female leads. She is called the matriarch.
explanations.description: An elephant family is made of mothers, daughters, sisters and their calves. Young males leave in their teens and live alone or with other males. So the adults who stay together for life are the females, and the oldest usually leads. What does she give the group? Karen McComb and her team tested this in Kenya and reported it in 2001. They played recorded calls of other elephants to elephant families. Families with older matriarchs were better at telling friends from strangers. They bunched together in defence at a stranger's call and stayed calm at a friend's call. Those families also had more calves. So the leader's memory helps everyone in her family. Spotted hyenas are different again. Hyena females are a little larger than the males, and almost every female outranks every male. A clan can have up to 80 members and is usually led by a female. A cub takes the rank just below their mother. Why females lead in hyenas is still argued over.
examples: An elephant calf is watched by her mother, her aunts and her older sisters.
A hyena cub born to the leading female outranks adult females who rank below the cub's mother.
In a troop of bonnet macaques or langurs, the daughters stay for life and the sons leave.
explanations.art: An old female elephant standing with her ears spread and her trunk raised, with younger females and calves bunched close behind her.

explanations.concept: Care is paid for in energy
explanations.definition: Every kind of care uses up energy from the parent's own body. Energy spent on one young is not available for the parent or for other young.
explanations.description: Energy is what a body needs to move, to keep warm and to grow. An animal gets energy only from food. Care always takes some. A sitting bird burns food to keep the eggs warm, and gives up time for feeding. A mammal mother turns her own body fat into milk. An elephant seal mother eats nothing for about 23 days while her pup drinks. An emperor penguin father stands through the Antarctic winter with one egg on his feet. He eats nothing for about 120 days, and may fall from about 38 kilograms to about 18. This is why care is called an investment. A parent's body has only so much energy. What goes to this chick cannot go to the next one, or to the parent's own safety. So parents in every species are pulled two ways, between the young they have now and the young they could have later. The different family systems are different ways of settling that pull.
examples: A seahorse mother's batch of eggs can use up about a third of her body weight.
A male elephant seal guarding a harem may also go without food for more than three months.
A turtle mother puts all her investment into the eggs, and none into care afterwards.
explanations.art: An emperor penguin father drawn twice: plump at the start of winter, and thin at the end, with the same egg on his feet in both.

explanations.concept: People: many hands raise a child
explanations.description: Humans are animals, so the same questions apply to us. A human child needs care for longer than almost any other young animal, about fifteen years or more. The scientist Sarah Blaffer Hrdy studied langur monkeys at Mount Abu in Rajasthan in the 1970s. She saw females other than the mother carrying infants. Later she asked how early human mothers could ever have raised such slow-growing children, often with a new baby arriving before the last child could find food alone. Her answer is that mothers never did it alone. Fathers, grandmothers, aunts, older brothers and sisters, and neighbours all fed and carried children. She calls this cooperative breeding, and many scientists now agree that people are cooperative breeders. It is still an idea about the distant past, and that is hard to test. Human families today come in many forms too. There are two parents, one parent, grandparents who raise grandchildren, joint families and adopted children. Children are raised well in all of these.
examples: In the Many Hands activity, you count how many different people looked after you in one day.
A paati who walks a child to the bus stop is doing what an elephant aunt does.

perspectives.explanation: Human children were always raised by many carers, not by the mother alone. Without helpers, our long childhood could not have arisen.
The bond between mother and father, and the father's help, mattered most. Helpers added to it.

explanations.art: A child in the middle of a ring of people: a mother, a father, a grandmother, an older sister, an uncle and a neighbour, each handing the child something or holding a hand.

explanations.concept: Female and male are not always fixed for life
explanations.definition: In some animals one individual makes both kinds of sex cell, or changes from one sex to the other, or becomes female or male depending on the warmth of the nest.
explanations.description: Because female and male are defined by sex cells, an animal's sex can be less fixed than we expect. An earthworm makes both egg cells and sperm, so each earthworm is both female and male. When two earthworms mate, each gives sperm to the other. All clownfish start life as males. In a group living at one sea anemone, the largest fish is the female and the second largest is her mate. If the female is removed, her mate changes into a female, and the next fish in size becomes the breeding male. In sea turtles, the sex of a hatchling is not decided when the egg is laid. It depends on how warm the sand is around the nest. For olive ridley turtles, who nest on the coasts of Odisha and Tamil Nadu, a nest at about 29 to 31 degrees gives about half females and half males. Warmer nests give more females and cooler nests more males. Scientists worry that as beaches warm, too few males will hatch.
examples: A garden snail, like an earthworm, is a hermaphrodite.
A clownfish who is a father this year may be a mother next year.
People who protect turtle nests on Chennai's beaches sometimes measure the warmth of the sand.
explanations.art: A sea anemone with three clownfish of different sizes, the largest labelled female and the second labelled male, and beside it a turtle nest in sand with a thermometer.

explanations.concept: Does the size of the sex cells decide the roles?
explanations.description: Scientists agree on what female and male mean. They disagree on how much follows from it. One side says the size of the sex cells pushes females and males in different directions in nearly all animals. Females start out having spent more on each young, so they tend to care and to choose, and males tend to compete. In 2016 Tim Janicke and his team put together 72 studies of 66 kinds of animals. On average, competition for partners was stronger among males. The other side says the push is weak, and that surroundings decide most of it. Hanna Kokko and Michael Jennions pointed out in 2008 that having spent more in the past is no reason, in itself, to spend more in future. They say care goes to whoever gains most by giving it, and that depends on things such as how many partners are free and how sure a parent is of being the parent. Patricia Gowaty showed in 2012 that a famous experiment behind the first view had a flaw. Both sides accept the facts in this lesson. They differ on how strong the pull of the sex cells is.
examples: For the first view: in most kinds of mammals, mothers do the caring and males compete.
For the second view: jacanas, seahorses and hyenas have the same two sizes of sex cell as cows, yet they have very different roles.

perspectives.explanation: Across 66 kinds of animals, competition for partners was on average stronger in males. The size of the sex cells sets a pattern, and surroundings can strengthen or weaken it.
Past spending does not decide future care. Who cares depends on what each parent gains or loses now, and that differs from species to species.
The fruit fly test that started the idea of eager males and choosy females was flawed. Roles vary much more than that idea allowed.

explanations.art: A seesaw with a large egg cell on one end and a tiny sperm on the other, and around it a pigeon pair, a jacana family and a seal harem.

agreed.text: An animal is female if they make the larger sex cells and male if they make the smaller ones. Nothing else defines the two sexes across all animals.
agreed.evidence: Egg cells and sperm have been measured in thousands of species. Animals whose roles are reversed, such as jacanas and seahorses, still have large egg cells in females and small sperm in males.

agreed.text: Sexual selection is real, and it works through both competing and choosing.
agreed.evidence: Darwin proposed it in 1871. Since then, experiments have changed tails, calls and colours and counted partners. Fights between males have been watched and scored in seals, deer and antelope.

agreed.text: When the father gives most of the care, the usual roles tend to swap.
agreed.evidence: In jacanas the males incubate and the larger females fight over territories. In Mormon crickets, where the male gives a big packet of food, Darryl Gwynne found in 1981 that males refuse most females.

agreed.text: Most kinds of birds raise their young as two parents, and most kinds of mammals do not.
agreed.evidence: Andrew Cockburn counted the bird families in 2006. Both parents care in about 81 of every 100 kinds of birds. Dieter Lukas and Tim Clutton-Brock found in 2013 that about 9 of every 100 kinds of mammals live as pairs.

agreed.text: Two birds who live as a pair are not always the only parents of the chicks in their nest.
agreed.evidence: DNA tests on chicks, reviewed by Simon Griffith and others in 2002, found chicks with an outside father in about nine out of ten kinds of birds tested.

agreed.text: In elephants, an older female leader helps her whole family.
agreed.evidence: Karen McComb's team played recorded elephant calls to families in Kenya. Families with older matriarchs told strangers from friends better, and had more calves. They published this in 2001.

challenging.claim: Males are eager by nature, and females are coy and faithful by nature.
challenging.who: Many biologists from 1948 until about the 1980s, following Angus Bateman's fruit fly test.
challenging.for: In many mammals and birds, males do court more openly, and females do refuse more often.
challenging.against: Females of many species seek several partners, as DNA tests on bird chicks showed. Jacana females fight for mates. When Bateman's test was repeated in 2012, the result did not hold.
challenging.context: For about forty years this was taught as a rule for all animals.

challenging.claim: In nature the male leads the group and the female follows.
challenging.who: A common belief, also found in many old nature books.
challenging.for: In gorillas, a silverback male does lead the group and settle quarrels.
challenging.against: Elephant families and hyena clans are led by females. Jacana females hold the territory. Many groups, such as pigeon pairs, have no leader at all.
challenging.context: This is a claim about all animals, drawn from a few well-known ones.

challenging.claim: The male in a harem is in charge of it.
challenging.who: A common way of describing harems.
challenging.for: A harem male does drive rival males away.
challenging.against: Many female elephant seals also mate at sea with males who hold no harem. A harem male may go without food for three months, and many males never win a harem at all.
challenging.context: This is about who really decides what happens in a group with one male and many females.

challenging.claim: If the father carries the young, the females must be the ones who compete.
challenging.who: Many books and websites about seahorses.
challenging.for: It is true of jacanas and of some pipefish, where females are brighter and fight for males.
challenging.against: In the seahorses that have been studied, males still compete more than females. They wrestle with their tails for partners.
challenging.context: This tests whether one rule can predict every family.

challenging.claim: A parent who has already spent more on a young should keep spending more.
challenging.who: Part of Robert Trivers's reasoning in 1972.
challenging.for: It feels sensible, and mothers who have spent more often do keep caring.
challenging.against: Richard Dawkins and Tamsin Carlisle showed in 1976 that this is a mistake in reasoning. What matters is what a parent would gain or lose from now on. What has already been spent cannot be got back.
challenging.context: The rest of Trivers's idea still stands. Only this one step was wrong.

challenging.claim: What other animals do shows what is right for people.
challenging.who: People on every side of arguments about families.
challenging.for: Humans are animals, and we can learn how bodies and families work by studying other animals.
challenging.against: Other animals do almost everything. Some pair for life, some keep harems, some leave their young at once. A fact about what happens cannot tell us what ought to happen.
challenging.context: This is about the difference between a finding and a rule.

big_questions.q: In the Warm Egg Test, was half the covering worth half the warmth? What does that tell you about a parent who must also eat?
big_questions.hint: Look at where your half-covered tumbler ended, and think about what the bare minutes did.

big_questions.q: If a father seahorse carries the young and gives birth, in what way is he still a father and not a mother?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the words female and male are defined by.

big_questions.q: Every young has one mother and one father. So how can males compete harder than females for partners?
big_questions.hint: Think about the average and about how evenly the young are shared out.

big_questions.q: A jacana mother leaves her eggs with the father and goes. Is she a bad mother? Is 'bad' a word that fits here at all?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether the chicks are cared for, and about who uses the word 'bad'.

big_questions.q: An elephant family follows the oldest female because of what she remembers. Who in your family remembers the most? What would be lost without them?
big_questions.hint: Think about a time someone older knew what to do because they had seen it before.

big_questions.q: Other animals live as pairs, harems, big groups and alone. Can any of them tell people how families should be?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between what happens and what is right.

big_questions.q: Scientists once called birds faithful because they saw pairs. DNA tests showed more. What else might we be sure of only because we cannot yet look closer?
big_questions.hint: Think about what we can see from outside and what a new tool might show.

story.title: The Big One Never Sits
story.note: A made-up story. Thamarai, her aunt Vasuki, her cousin Kathir, the village tank and the kite are imagined. The birds are real. Bronze-winged jacanas walk on floating leaves on ponds across India. The female is much heavier than the male and holds a stretch of pond with one to four mates. She lays four eggs for each mate. The male alone sits on the eggs for about 29 days and looks after the chicks. He calls loudly to bring the female to him, and he carries the chicks under his wings when there is danger.
text: The first page of Chithi's notebook had a rule on it, written in green ink. 'Write what you saw. Write what you guessed. Never mix the two.' Thamarai read the rule, nodded, and broke it within the hour.

The tank lay behind the village, and after the August rain half of it was covered in lotus leaves. Vasuki Chithi, her mother's younger sister, counted the birds here every monsoon for a wetland survey. This year she had a sprained ankle and a niece on holiday. 'You will be my legs,' she said. She hung the binoculars around Thamarai's neck and gave her the notebook. 'Find the jacana nests. Then tell me who is who.'

The jacanas were easy to find. They were dark birds with bronze-brown wings, and they walked on the lotus leaves as if the pond were a floor. Their toes were as long as Thamarai's fingers. By noon she had found three nests. Each was a small wet heap of weeds on the leaves, and on each heap a bird sat. A fourth bird walked around all three. That bird was much bigger than the others. When a strange jacana landed at the far end, the big one ran at the stranger with both wings raised, and the stranger left.
Thamarai sat on the bund and wrote. 'Three mothers on three nests. One father, very big, guards them all. He is like a king with three queens.'
Chithi read the page. She said nothing. She turned to the first page and tapped the rule.
'But it is obvious,' said Thamarai. 'The big strong one is the father. The ones on the eggs are the mothers.'
'What did you see?'
'Three small ones sitting. One big one walking about and chasing.'
'Then that is what you write. Nest three has only one egg so far. Come at first light tomorrow, and watch how the second one arrives.'

At first light the tank was grey, and mist lay on the water. The small bird at nest three was standing beside the heap of weeds. The bird stretched up and called. It was a loud, rough yell, and it came again and again. Across the leaves, the big bird turned and came walking.
The two of them stood together for a while. Then the big bird stepped on to the heap, settled low, and was very still.
Thamarai held her breath. She did not know why.

The big bird stood up, shook, and walked away across the leaves without looking back. Where one egg had been, there were two. The small bird stepped on to the heap, pushed both eggs under his belly, and sat.
Thamarai lowered the binoculars. She looked at what she had written the day before. Then she walked back along the bund to where Chithi sat with her foot up on a stool.
'The big one laid the egg,' she said. 'I saw it. The big one is the mother.'
'Of nest three,' said Chithi. 'And nests one and two?'
Thamarai opened her mouth and shut it again. 'I don't know,' she said slowly. 'I did not see those eggs laid.'
Chithi smiled for the first time that week. 'That is the best sentence you have said so far. Write it down.'

She watched for nine more mornings. Two more eggs came to nest three, each one after a visit from the big bird. The big bird never sat for longer than it took to lay. The small bird sat through the rain. He left only for a few minutes at a time to feed, and he ran back across the leaves each time as if the eggs were calling him. Chithi told her the rest in the evenings. Among jacanas the female is the larger one. She holds the whole stretch of pond and keeps other females out. She may have four mates, and she lays four eggs for each.
'So she is not a king with three queens,' said Thamarai. 'What is she, then?'
'What have you seen her do?'
'Lay eggs. Chase strangers. Walk about.'
'And him?'
'Sit,' said Thamarai. 'Sit, and sit, and sit.'

Nest one hatched in the third week. Four chicks came out on legs that looked too long for them. They followed the small bird across the leaves, pecking at whatever he pecked at. Thamarai was drawing them when a shadow slid over the tank. A kite had dropped low and was turning above the lotus.

She stood up and shouted before she knew she was going to. The small bird crouched. The chicks ran to him, and then there were no chicks at all. He stood up and walked quickly towards the reeds. From under each of his wings hung two pairs of thin legs, swinging as he went.

Thamarai laughed out loud. Then she sat down again and was quiet for some time. She opened the notebook at her first day. She did not cross anything out. Beside it she wrote in small letters: 'Guessed, and wrong. I thought big meant father and sitting meant mother. Seen: the big one lays the eggs. The small ones sit on them and carry the chicks.'
That evening her cousin Kathir, who was seven, came running along the bund and pointed. 'Look, the mother bird is taking her babies for a walk!'
Thamarai took the binoculars from around her neck and put them around his. 'Come tomorrow at first light,' she said. 'And bring a pencil.'
story.epiphany: Thamarai decided who was the mother and who was the father from their size and from who sat on the eggs. Then she watched an egg being laid. Among jacanas the larger bird who guards the pond is the female. The smaller birds who sit on the eggs and carry the chicks are the males.
ask: What would you need to see before you could say which bird is the female?
The mother jacana lays the eggs and then leaves them. How are the chicks still looked after?
Why might it help a jacana mother to be free of sitting, on a pond where many nests are lost?
Think of something you were sure of from how it looked. How could you check it?
Which of the things in your own day are things you saw, and which are things you guessed?

roots.context: In the Warm Egg Test you found out what an egg loses each time the sitter leaves. You also met fathers who carry the young and mothers who lead. Now we ask what this tells us about the words mother and father, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Warm Egg Test, the tumbler covered for half the time cooled much more than the one always covered. A bird's egg needs a sitter nearly all the time, and either parent can sit. So in most birds both parents care, and among jacanas the father sits alone. An animal is female or male only by the size of the sex cells they make. Who cares for the young depends on what the young need and who can give it.
deep_truth.habit: We use the word mother to mean the one who looks after the young, and father to mean the one who fights or goes away. We treat those jobs as part of being female or male. The science defines female and male only by sex cells, and it finds the jobs shared out in every possible way.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Warm Egg Test the bare minutes cost the tumbler warmth that the covered minutes could not put back. A pigeon father and mother take turns for that reason. A calf needs milk, which only the mother makes, so cattle fathers give no care. A seahorse father has the pouch, so he carries.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal whose kind raises children with many hands. You are here because several people spent their time and energy on you.
three.what_is_life: No life goes on to the next generation unless someone gives up part of their own energy for the young. Different animals share out that giving in different ways.
three.what_is_this_world: The world has no single correct family. A pond, a beach, a tree hollow and a herd each led to a different one.

roots.thread: The first living beings that mixed their instructions made sex cells of one size. From that one kind came two kinds, large and small. From those two kinds came every family in this lesson: the pair of pigeons, the seal harem, the jacana mother with four mates, the seahorse father with a pouch and the elephant grandmother. They look very different. Under each of them are the same two cells and the same need, which is that someone must spend energy on the young.

teachings.teaching: As paraphrased: in the beginning the Self was alone, and was as large as a woman and a man holding each other. The Self divided into two, and from the two halves came wife and husband.
teachings.link: The Upanishad says female and male came from one being who was both. Science says the two sizes of sex cell came from one earlier size. The two accounts are different kinds of statement, but both begin with one and arrive at two.
verse: स वै नैव रेमे । तस्मादेकाकी न रमते । स द्वितीयमैच्छत्।
स हैतावानास यथा स्त्रीपुमांसौ सम्परिष्वक्तौ । स इममेवात्मानं द्वेधापातयत्।

teachings.teaching: As paraphrased: know the male, but keep to the female, and be like a valley that all the streams of the world run into.
teachings.link: Lao Tzu asks one person to hold both. A jacana father who guards his patch and also warms the eggs does both jobs in one body, and so does a clownfish who is father one year and mother the next.
verse: 知其雄，守其雌，為天下谿。
為天下谿，常德不離，復歸於嬰兒。

teachings.teaching: As paraphrased: as a mother would guard her only child with her life, so let a person grow a heart without limit towards all beings.
teachings.link: The Buddha takes a mother's care as the model, and then asks everyone to give it. In nature too, care is given by fathers, aunts, sisters and helpers, and is not the mother's alone.

science.text: Female and male are defined by the size of the sex cells. In different species the young are cared for by the mother, the father, both, a group, or nobody.
The first sex cells were probably all one size, and the two sizes arose later.
How strongly the size of the sex cells pushes females towards caring and males towards competing is still argued over.

other_view.who: Tim Janicke and other biologists who study sexual selection across many species
other_view.view: They say the roles are not open to every arrangement equally. In the 66 kinds of animals they compared, males on average competed more and females cared more. They trace this to the sex cells themselves. In their view jacanas and seahorses are real, but they are exceptions to a pattern that the sex cells set.

practice.title: Whose hands?
practice.say: Sit still and breathe slowly three times. Look at your hands. Think of one thing somebody did for you today before you asked. Who was it? Now think of someone smaller than you, such as a brother, a plant or a bird at the window. What is one thing your hands could do for them today? Breathe once more, and then go and do it.
practice.kid: Sit still. Breathe slowly three times. Look at your hands. Who did something for you today before you asked? Who is smaller than you and near you? What could your hands do for them today? Go and do it.

ask: If mother means the one who makes the egg cells, what word would you use for the one who does the caring?
Who looked after you today, and did any of them have to give something up to do it?
A jacana and a cow have the same two kinds of sex cell and very different families. What does that tell you?
roots.art: A child sitting on a floor mat looking at her open hands, with a pigeon on a nest on the window ledge behind her and a grandmother in the doorway.

games.title: Stay or Go? The two-parent game
games.context: This is a game for two players, who are the mother and the father of the same young. On each card both secretly choose to stay and care, or to go. You find out that the best choice changes with what the young need.

printables.title: 8 animal cards, with what real animals do on the back

items.f: ROCK PIGEON. Young points: both stay 4. Only one stays 1. Nobody stays 0. Bonus if you go: mother +1, father +1.
items.b: Real pigeons: both stay. They take turns to sit on the eggs, and both make crop milk for the chicks.

items.f: EMPEROR PENGUIN. Young points: both stay 3. Only one stays 0. Nobody stays 0. Bonus if you go: mother +1, father +1.
items.b: Real emperor penguins: both stay. The father holds the egg for about two months without eating. The mother returns with food as the chick hatches. If either fails, the chick dies.

items.f: ELEPHANT SEAL. Young points: both stay 2. Only mother stays 2. Only father stays 0. Nobody stays 0. Bonus if you go: mother +0, father +3.
items.b: Real elephant seals: the mother stays and the father goes. The pup needs only milk. The father gains more by guarding other females.

items.f: KING COBRA. Young points: both stay 4. Only mother stays 4. Only father stays 0. Nobody stays 1. Bonus if you go: mother +1, father +2.
items.b: Real king cobras: the mother builds a nest of dry leaves and guards the eggs. The father leaves.

items.f: BRONZE-WINGED JACANA. Young points: both stay 3. Only one stays 3. Nobody stays 0. Bonus if you go: mother +3, father +0.
items.b: Real jacanas: the father stays and the mother goes. She lays another clutch for another mate. He would find very few free females if he left.

items.f: GIANT WATER BUG. Young points: both stay 4. Only father stays 4. Only mother stays 0. Nobody stays 0. Bonus if you go: mother +2, father +0.
items.b: Real giant water bugs: the mother glues the eggs on to the father's back. He carries them until they hatch. She goes to feed and make more eggs.

items.f: SEAHORSE. Young points: both stay 3. Only father stays 3. Only mother stays 0. Nobody stays 0. Bonus if you go: mother +2, father +0.
items.b: Real seahorses: the father carries the eggs in his pouch. The mother feeds and makes the next batch, and visits him each morning.

items.f: OLIVE RIDLEY TURTLE. Young points: both stay 2. Only one stays 2. Nobody stays 2. Bonus if you go: mother +2, father +2.
items.b: Real olive ridley turtles: nobody stays. The mother buries about a hundred eggs in the sand and returns to the sea. The father never comes ashore.

printables.title: Score sheet for two players: eight rounds

rules: Two players. Cut out the 8 cards and shuffle them, with the animal side up. Each player needs one coin. If you have no printer, copy the cards by hand on slips of paper.
One player is the mother and the other is the father. Swap after four cards.
Turn up the top card and read the animal side aloud. Do not look at the back yet.
Each player secretly sets a coin under one hand. Heads means 'I stay and care'. Tails means 'I go'. Do not talk about your choice.
Lift your hands together. Find the young points for what you both chose. Both players get those points, because the young belong to both of you.
A player who chose 'go' also adds their own bonus. Write both totals on the score sheet.
Now turn the card over and read what the real animals do. Say whether you chose as they do.
After eight cards, the player with more points wins. Then say which cards made you both stay, and why.

setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the eight cards. Each player takes a coin. Decide who is the mother first.

setup.caption: 2. Read the card. Secretly set your coin: heads for stay, tails for go.

setup.art: Two hands lifted to show one coin heads up and one coin tails up, and a pencil writing points on the score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Show together. Add the young points, and the bonus for anyone who went.
