flow.do: Cut out or copy the 8 cards. Shuffle them with the animal side up. Give each player a coin. Draw the score sheet. Decide who is the mother for the first four cards.
flow.say: We are the two parents of the same young. On each card we each choose to stay or to go. Let us read the rules together.
flow.kid: Shuffle the cards. Take a coin. Decide who is the mother first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stay or Go. You set up the cards and learn the rules.
flow.parent: Read the pigeon card aloud as an example before you start. Work out together what each of you would score for all four pairs of choices. That one worked example makes the rest easy.

flow.do: Play four cards. For each, read the card, set the coins in secret, show together and write the points. Then turn the card over and read the back.
flow.say: Read the card. Think about what the young need and what you gain by going. Set your coin. Ready? Show.
flow.kid: Read the card. Set your coin in secret. Show together. Write the points.
flow.context: In this step of Stay or Go you play the first four cards.

ask.q: What did you look at on the card before you chose?
good: How many points the young get if I stay.
Whether the young do just as well with one parent.
How big my bonus is if I go.

flow.parent: Play to win. If you always stay, your child learns nothing about why real animals leave. After each card ask your child for the reason for their choice before you give yours.

flow.do: Swap roles. Play the last four cards in the same way. Add up the two totals.
flow.say: Now you are the father and I am the mother. Look carefully at whose bonus is bigger on each card.
flow.kid: Swap roles. Play four more cards. Add up your points.
flow.context: In this step of Stay or Go you swap roles and finish the game.
flow.parent: On the penguin card, both players do best by staying, but only if each trusts the other to stay. Notice aloud if one of you went and the chick was lost.

flow.do: Lay out all eight cards. Sort them into four groups by what the real animals do: both stay, mother stays, father stays, nobody stays. Ask what the cards in each group share.
flow.say: Let us sort the cards by what the real animals do. What is the same about the cards where both parents stay?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into four groups: both stay, mother stays, father stays, nobody stays.
flow.context: In this step you sort the Stay or Go cards and look for the pattern.

ask.q: What is the same about the cards where both parents stay?
good: The young get far fewer points with only one parent.
One parent alone cannot do the job.

ask.q: On the cards where one parent goes, which parent is it?
good: The one with the bigger bonus for going.
The one the young can manage without.

check.q: On the jacana card, why does the mother go and the father stay?
options: She gains a lot by going, and he gains nothing
The mother does not like the eggs
check.why: One parent is enough for the eggs. The mother can lay another clutch for another mate, so her bonus is large. The father would find few free females, so his bonus is zero. If you chose the second answer, look at the card again: either parent alone scores 3.

flow.think: What would have to change on the elephant seal card for the father to stay?

experiments.title: The Warm Egg Test: what does an egg lose when the sitter leaves?
experiments.context: In this test you find out how much warmth eggs lose when a parent leaves the nest. Three steel tumblers of warm water stand in for three nests of eggs. One is covered all the time, one is covered for half the time, and one is never covered. After 20 minutes you find out how much warmth each has lost.
experiments.question: How much warmth does an 'egg' lose if the cover is on all the time, half the time, or never? Is the half-covered tumbler nearer to the always-covered one or to the bare one?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Put the three tumblers in order from warmest to coolest at the end. Then guess whether the half-covered tumbler will end nearer to the always-covered one or nearer to the bare one. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: All three tumblers are the same size and are filled to the same level from one jug, so they start equally warm. They stand on the same folded newspaper, away from a fan, a window and the stove. The two covers are the same kind of lid and the same kind of cloth. Only the time under cover is different.

materials.item: steel tumblers of the same size
a jug of warm water, about as warm as a bath you would enjoy
small steel lids or saucers that cover a tumbler
hand towels or kitchen cloths of the same kind
a folded newspaper to stand the tumblers on
a timer, such as the one on a phone
a kitchen thermometer or a digital fever thermometer, if you have one
three paper slips marked A, B and C, and the results table drawn on paper

experiments.safety: A grown-up mixes the warm water. It should be warm bath water, about 40 degrees, and never hot enough to hurt a finger held in it. Do not use water straight from a kettle.

schedule.what: Guess, fill three tumblers, cover A always, B half the time and C never for 20 minutes, then measure and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Write the warmth of each tumbler at the start and after 20 minutes, and take one from the other to find the warmth lost. If you have no thermometer, write the order from warmest to coolest that the blind finger test gave.

example_chart.title: Example: degrees lost in 20 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show what a chart of results looks like. Yours will be different.

setup.art: Three identical steel tumblers in a row on a folded newspaper, labelled A, B and C with paper slips, and a jug of water beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three tumblers to the same level from one jug of warm water.

setup.art: Tumbler A with a steel lid on top and a hand towel wrapped around it, tumbler B being covered the same way, and tumbler C left bare.
setup.caption: 2. Cover A and B with a lid and a cloth. Leave C bare. Start the timer.

setup.art: A child lifting the lid and cloth off tumbler B while looking at a phone timer that shows 5 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Every 5 minutes, change B: cover off, then on, then off.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut dipping one finger of each hand into two tumblers, while a parent holds a thermometer in the third.
setup.caption: 4. After 20 minutes, measure all three, or compare them by finger with eyes shut.

flow.do: Show the three empty tumblers, the lids and the cloths. Explain what will happen to each tumbler. Ask for both guesses and the reason. Write the guesses above the table. Do not say whether you agree.
flow.say: Each tumbler of warm water is a clutch of eggs. A is covered all the time. B is covered for half the time. C is never covered. Which will end warmest? Will B end nearer to A or nearer to C? Why?
flow.kid: A is always covered. B is covered half the time. C is bare. Guess which one ends warmest and which ends coolest.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Warm Egg Test. You guess before you test.

ask.q: Will B end nearer to A, nearer to C, or exactly in the middle? Why do you think so?
good: In the middle, because it is covered half the time.
Nearer to C, because the heat that leaves does not come back.
Nearer to A, because the cloth stays warm.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good start. Most children get the order right. The second guess is the real question, and nobody at the table knows the answer yet.

flow.do: Mix warm water in a jug, about as warm as a nice bath. Fill the three tumblers to one finger-width below the rim. Stand them on the folded newspaper with their A, B and C slips. Measure each with the thermometer, or feel each with a finger. Rule a table on paper with rows A, B and C and columns Start and After 20 minutes. Write the start in it.
flow.say: I will mix the water. You fill the three tumblers to the same level. Now measure each one. Are they the same at the start?
flow.kid: Fill the three tumblers to the same level. Measure or feel each one. Write each start in your table.
flow.context: In this step of the Warm Egg Test you fill the tumblers and check that they start equally warm.
flow.parent: A fever thermometer reads only from about 32 to 42 degrees. If you use one, start with water at 40 to 42 degrees. Dip only the tip, and wait for the beep. If the three starts differ by more than half a degree, pour them all back into the jug and fill again.

flow.do: Put a lid on A and wrap a cloth around it. Do the same to B. Leave C bare. Start a 20-minute timer. Your child is the timekeeper for B. At 5 minutes they take B's lid and cloth off. At 10 minutes they put them back. At 15 minutes they take them off again.
flow.say: You are the parent of tumbler B. At 5 minutes you leave to feed, so take the cover off. At 10 minutes you come back. At 15 minutes you leave again. Do not touch A or C at all.
flow.kid: Cover A and B. Leave C bare. At 5 minutes uncover B. At 10 cover it. At 15 uncover it again. Watch the timer.
flow.context: In this step of the Warm Egg Test you wait 20 minutes and change tumbler B's cover every 5 minutes.

ask.q: If these were real eggs, which tumbler has a parent who stays all the time? Which has a parent who leaves half the time? Which has no parent?
good: A has two parents who take turns, so the eggs are never bare.
B has one parent who must leave to find food.
C has nobody sitting.

flow.parent: Keep the room as it is: no fan switched on or off halfway. When B is uncovered, put its lid and cloth down beside it, not on top of another tumbler.

flow.do: When the timer rings, take all covers off. Measure A, then B, then C, with the thermometer. With no thermometer, your child shuts their eyes. You slide two tumblers in front of them. They dip one finger of each hand and say which is warmer. Do all three pairs. Write the results.
flow.say: Time is up. Measure each one and write it down. Now take each end number away from its start number. That is the warmth lost. Which lost the most? Which lost the least?
flow.kid: Measure A, B and C. Write each one down. Work out how much warmth each lost.
flow.context: In this step of the Warm Egg Test you measure the three tumblers after 20 minutes.
flow.parent: Measure quickly, because the uncovered tumblers go on cooling. With the finger test, mix up the tumblers so that your child cannot tell which is which. If a fever thermometer shows 'Lo', the water is below about 32 degrees. Write 'below 32'.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Your child writes three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why. Only after that, read them the explanation in the parent note.
flow.say: Look at your three numbers. Where did B end, nearer to A or nearer to C? Tell me why you think so.
flow.kid: Write three sentences: what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.context: In this step you say what the results of the Warm Egg Test show.

ask.q: What did B lose in the bare minutes? Did the covered minutes give it back?
good: B lost warmth each time I took the cover off.
The cover only slowed the loss. It did not warm the water again.
B ended between A and C.

ask.q: A real bird who sits alone must leave to eat. What could a second parent change?
good: The second parent can sit while the first one feeds.
The eggs would never be bare, like tumbler A.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. A cover does not make warmth. It only slows the loss, so whatever warmth leaves in the bare minutes is gone. Your tumbler B usually ends somewhere between A and C. Whether it is nearer to A or to C depends on your room, and either is a fair result. A real bird does add warmth from her or his own body when sitting, which a cloth cannot do. But the bird must first eat to make that warmth, and must warm the eggs up again after every trip away. This is why two pigeons take turns on one nest, and why a hornbill father feeds the mother while she stays inside. If all three tumblers ended almost the same, your room is very warm. Run the test again for 30 minutes, or near a fan that blows on all three equally.
flow.think: A calf grows inside the mother for nine months. Who keeps the calf warm, and can the father take a turn?

experiments.title: The One Guard Test: how many can one guard hold on to?
experiments.context: In this test one person guards 12 coins with one hand while another tries to take them. You try it with the coins close together, spread out, and spread far apart. A harem is one male with many females. You will find out why some animals have harems and others live as pairs.
experiments.question: How many of 12 coins can one guard keep for 30 seconds when the coins are close together, spread out, or far apart?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. How many of the 12 coins will the guard still have after 30 seconds in each of the three layouts? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same person guards in every try and the same person takes, because people differ in speed. Every try lasts 30 seconds. The taker follows the same rules each time. Each layout is tried three times, because one try can be a fluke. Only how far apart the coins are is different.

materials.item: coins or bottle caps of the same kind
a clear patch of floor, about two big steps wide
a dinner plate and a sheet of newspaper, to mark the sizes of the layouts
a small bowl for the taker's 'home'
a timer, and the results table drawn on paper

experiments.safety: Play kneeling on the floor, not at a table edge. The guard taps the back of the taker's hand gently with open fingers. No grabbing, slapping or pushing. Keep heads apart.

schedule.what: Guess, then guard 12 coins for 30 seconds in three layouts, three tries each, and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Write the coins the guard still has after each 30-second try. For each layout, circle the middle of the three numbers.

example_chart.title: Example: coins the guard kept, out of 12 (middle of three tries)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show what a chart of results looks like. Yours will be different.

setup.art: Twelve coins in a tight group on the floor, the size of a dinner plate, with a child kneeling beside them holding one hand above the coins.
setup.caption: 1. Close layout: 12 coins in a group the size of a dinner plate. The guard uses one hand.

setup.art: A second person kneeling opposite, sliding one coin away with one finger towards a small bowl behind her.
setup.caption: 2. The taker slides one coin at a time to the home bowl. A tapped taker goes home empty-handed.

setup.art: The same twelve coins now spread out over an open sheet of newspaper on the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Spread layout: the coins spread over a whole sheet of newspaper.

setup.art: The same twelve coins scattered over a patch of floor two big steps wide, with the guard stretching to reach.
setup.caption: 4. Far layout: the coins scattered two big steps wide. Count what the guard keeps each time.

flow.do: Show the three layouts with the plate, the newspaper and two big steps. Explain the rules. Ask for a guess for each layout, and the reason. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: You will guard 12 coins with one hand for 30 seconds. I will try to take them. How many will you keep when they are close? Spread out? Far apart? Why?
flow.kid: You guard 12 coins with one hand. Guess how many you keep each time. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the One Guard Test. You guess before you test.

ask.q: In which layout will guarding be hardest, and why?
good: Far apart, because my hand cannot be everywhere.
Far apart, because the taker can go where I am not.

flow.parent: Decide who guards and who takes, and keep to it for the whole test. A child usually enjoys guarding. You can swap for a second full test afterwards.

flow.do: Agree the rules and try them once slowly. The guard kneels and uses one hand. The taker uses one finger to slide one coin at a time to the home bowl behind them. If the guard taps the back of the taker's hand, the taker drops the coin and touches the bowl before trying again.
flow.say: One hand for you, one finger for me, one coin at a time. If you tap my hand, I go home with nothing. Let us try it slowly once.
flow.kid: Guard with one hand. A tap sends the taker home. Try it slowly once.
flow.context: In this step of the One Guard Test you agree the rules and practise once.
flow.parent: The home bowl should be an arm's length behind the taker, so that every trip takes a moment. Keep the taps gentle. A coin that was dropped goes back where it was.

flow.do: Do three tries of 30 seconds with the close layout. After each, count the coins the guard still has and write it. Then do three tries with the spread layout, and three with the far layout. Rest between tries.
flow.say: Thirty seconds, starting now. Stop. How many coins do you still have? Write it down. Now we set them out again.
flow.kid: Guard for 30 seconds. Count your coins. Write the number. Do every layout three times.
flow.context: In this step of the One Guard Test you run nine short tries and write the results.
flow.parent: Take as many as you fairly can, in the same way each time. If you go easy in one layout, the test shows nothing. In the far layout the guard may move about on their knees.

flow.do: Circle the middle number for each layout. Your child writes what I think, what I saw, and why. Only after that, give the explanation in the parent note.
flow.say: Look at your middle numbers. What changed as the coins moved apart? Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Circle the middle number for each layout. Then write what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.context: In this step you say what the results of the One Guard Test show.

ask.q: What changed as the coins moved further apart?
good: I kept fewer coins.
My hand could not reach the far ones in time.
The taker went wherever I was not.

ask.q: Female seals crowd together on one small beach. Female pigeons nest far apart across a city. Which is like which layout?
good: The seals are like the close layout, so one male can guard many.
The pigeons are like the far layout, so one male cannot guard several.

check.q: Why can one male elephant seal keep many females, but a male pigeon cannot?
options: Female seals gather closely, so one male can guard them
Pigeons do not want many partners
check.why: One guard can hold many only when they are close together, as you found with the coins. Female seals crowd on to a few beaches. Female pigeons are spread out, each at a nest. If you chose strength, remember that the strongest guard still lost coins in the far layout.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. Stephen Emlen and Lewis Oring said in 1977 that harems arise where females, or the food and nesting places they need, are gathered closely enough for one animal to guard. Where they are spread out, an animal who tried to guard several partners would lose them all, and does better with one. The coins are a model. Real females are not coins. They move, and they choose, and many female seals also mate with males away from the harem.
flow.think: The coins could not walk away or choose. What would change if they could?

activities.title: Who Looks After the Young? Guess first
activities.context: In this activity you guess who looks after the young in eight animal families: the mother, the father, both, a group or nobody. Then you find out, and count your surprises.

materials.item: paper and a pencil

activities.record: Keep the list of eight animals with your guesses and the real answers. Under it, write the one answer that surprised you most and one question you now have.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with eight animal names in a column and two more columns headed 'My guess' and 'Really'.
setup.caption: 1. Write the eight animals in a column. Add columns for 'My guess' and 'Really'.

setup.art: A child writing the word 'Both' beside 'Pigeon' while a parent holds a phone with the answers turned away.
setup.caption: 2. For each animal, guess: mother, father, both, group or nobody.

setup.art: The same sheet with the 'Really' column filled in and three of the rows circled.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in the real answers. Circle every surprise.

flow.do: Your child writes these eight animals in a column: rock pigeon, bronze-winged jacana, seahorse, elephant, emperor penguin, olive ridley turtle, great hornbill, elephant seal. Beside each they write a guess: mother, father, both, group or nobody. Ask for the reason for any two.
flow.say: Here are eight animals. For each one, who looks after the eggs or the young? Write mother, father, both, group or nobody. Tell me why for two of them.
flow.kid: Write the eight animals. Guess who looks after the young of each. Say why for two.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Looks After the Young. You guess before you find out.

ask.q: What made you guess 'mother' for that one?
good: Mothers usually look after babies.
The mother lays the eggs, so she stays with them.
I have seen a picture of it.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess yet. Most children write 'mother' for most of the list, and that is the starting point this lesson needs.

flow.do: Read out the real answers one at a time from the parent note. Your child writes each in the 'Really' column and circles each surprise.
flow.say: Here is what really happens. Write each answer down. Put a circle around every one that surprises you.
flow.kid: Write the real answers. Circle each one that surprises you.
flow.context: In this step of Who Looks After the Young you find out the real answers.
flow.parent: Rock pigeon: both, taking turns on the eggs. Bronze-winged jacana: the father alone. Seahorse: the father carries the eggs in a pouch, and nobody cares for the young after birth. Elephant: the mother with a group of aunts and sisters. Emperor penguin: the father alone holds the egg through the winter, then both feed the chick. Olive ridley turtle: nobody, after the mother buries the eggs. Great hornbill: both, with the mother sealed inside the nest and the father bringing food. Elephant seal: the mother alone.

flow.do: Your child counts how many animals fall under mother, father, both, group and nobody. Ask what they notice and what they wonder. They write one question.
flow.say: Count how many are mother, father, both, group and nobody. What do you notice? What do you wonder? Write one question you want answered.
flow.kid: Count each kind of answer. Then write one question you have.
flow.context: In this step of Who Looks After the Young you look for a pattern and write a question.

ask.q: What do you notice, and what do you wonder?
good: It is not always the mother.
Birds often have both parents.
Why does the father do it in some animals?
Why does nobody look after the turtles?

flow.parent: Do not answer the question yet. The Warm Egg Test and the explanation cards answer it. Keep the page, so your child can come back to their question at the end.

activities.title: Size Detective: what does body size say about a family?
activities.context: In this activity you compare the weights of females and males in seven animals. Then you look for a link between the size difference and the kind of family. Darwin compared species in this way. You will find out whether a big size difference points to a kind of family.

materials.item: paper, a pencil and a ruler
a calculator, such as the one on a phone

activities.record: Keep the table of seven animals with the 'times as heavy' column filled in. Under it, write the pattern you found in one sentence, and one animal that does not fit neatly.

setup.art: A hand-drawn table with columns headed Animal, Male weight, Female weight, 'Male is how many times as heavy?' and Family.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the table of seven animals with the weights of males and females.

setup.art: A child dividing 180 by 90 on a phone calculator and writing '2' in the table.
setup.caption: 2. Divide the male's weight by the female's weight for each animal.

setup.art: Seven paper slips with animal names laid in a row on a table, from a seal at one end to a jacana at the other.
setup.caption: 3. Put the animals in order by that number. Look at the family beside each.

flow.do: Your child copies the table from the parent note, leaving the 'times as heavy' column empty. Before any sums, ask in which kinds of family they expect males to be much heavier than females, and why.
flow.say: Copy this table. Before you work anything out, guess. In which families will the males be much heavier than the females? Why?
flow.kid: Copy the table. Leave the last column empty.
flow.context: This is the first step of Size Detective. You copy the weights and guess the pattern.

ask.q: Where do you expect males to be much heavier, and why?
good: Where males fight each other, because the big ones win.
Where one male has many partners.

flow.parent: The table, in kilograms: southern elephant seal, male 3,300, female 600, one male with many females. Gorilla, male 180, female 90, one male with several females. Blackbuck, male 38, female 27, males defend patches. Sarus crane, male 6.7, female 5.3, pair. Spotted hyena, male 68, female 69, big group led by females. Pheasant-tailed jacana, male 0.13, female 0.14, one female with several males. Bronze-winged jacana, male 0.18, female 0.28, one female with several males. These are typical figures from single studies, and animals vary.

flow.do: For each animal, your child divides the male's weight by the female's weight on a calculator. They write the answer to one decimal place. Then they list the animals in order, from the largest answer to the smallest.
flow.say: Divide the male's weight by the female's weight. A number above 1 means the male is heavier. A number below 1 means the female is heavier. Now put them in order.
flow.kid: Divide the male's weight by the female's. Write each answer. Put the animals in order.
flow.context: In this step of Size Detective you work out how many times as heavy the male is.
flow.parent: The answers are about 5.5 for the seal, 2 for the gorilla, 1.4 for the blackbuck, 1.3 for the crane, 1.0 for the hyena, 0.9 for the pheasant-tailed jacana and 0.6 for the bronze-winged jacana.

flow.do: Your child reads down the ordered list with the family beside each animal. Ask what pattern they see, and which animal fits least well. Then read the parent note aloud.
flow.say: Read down your list. What kind of family is at the top? What kind is at the bottom? Which animal does not fit neatly?
flow.kid: Read down your ordered list. Look at the family beside each animal.
flow.context: In this step of Size Detective you look for the link between size and family.

good: Where one male has many females, the male is much heavier.
In pairs, the two are nearly the same.
Where females have several mates, the female is heavier.

check.q: A newly found animal has males three times as heavy as females. Which family is most likely?
options: A pair who share the care
check.why: Where a few males win most of the partners by fighting, big males have the most young, so males become much heavier over many generations. In pairs, the two sexes are usually close in size. If you chose the third answer, look at the jacanas: there the females are the heavier ones.

flow.parent: The pattern: the sex that fights for many partners is the heavier one. It is a tendency and not a law. Hyena females lead and are only slightly heavier. In many spiders, fish and insects the females are larger because a bigger body can make more eggs, which has nothing to do with fighting.

activities.title: Many Hands: who looked after you yesterday?
activities.context: In this activity you list everything that was done for you in one day and who did it. You find out how many carers one human child has. Sarah Blaffer Hrdy says that people have always raised children this way.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
scraps of paper for names

activities.record: Keep the list of what was done for you and by whom, the tally for each person, and your ring of names, or a photo of it. Write the number of carers at the top.

setup.art: A notebook page with a list down the left side: 'woke me', 'made idli', 'plaited my hair', 'walked me to the bus', each with a name beside it.
setup.caption: 1. List everything someone did for you yesterday, from waking to sleeping. Write who did it.

setup.art: A tally chart with names such as Amma, Appa, Paati, Akka and 'bus driver', with tally marks beside each.
setup.caption: 2. Make a tally mark for each person. Count the carers.

setup.art: A drawing of a child in the centre of a ring of people, with a line from each person to the child.
setup.caption: 3. Put your name in the middle and each carer's name in a ring around it.

flow.do: Your child thinks through yesterday from waking to sleeping. They list each thing that someone did for them, and who did it. Include food, washing, travel, teaching, comfort and keeping them safe. Help them to remember, but let them write.
flow.say: Think through yesterday from waking up to falling asleep. What did someone do for you? Who did it? Write each one down.
flow.kid: Think through yesterday. List what people did for you. Write who did each thing.
flow.context: This is the first step of Many Hands. You list what was done for you in one day.

ask.q: Who helped you without being in your family?
good: My teacher.
The auto driver or bus driver.
Our neighbour.
The person who cooked or sold our food.

flow.parent: Before they start, ask your child to guess how many different people they will list. Most children guess two or three and find six or more.

flow.do: Your child makes a tally mark for each person and counts the carers. Then they write their own name on a sheet of paper. They write each carer's name on a scrap and set the scraps in a ring around it.
flow.say: Give each person a tally mark for each thing they did. How many different people are there? Now set their names in a ring around yours.
flow.kid: Tally each person. Count the carers. Set their names in a ring around yours.
flow.context: In this step of Many Hands you count your carers and draw them.
flow.parent: The tally is not a score of who loves the child most. If your child starts to rank people, say that the count shows who had the time that day.

flow.do: Tell your child who looked after you when you were their age. If a grandparent is near or on the phone, ask them too. Compare the numbers. Then tell them that Sarah Blaffer Hrdy, who studies human families, says people have always raised children together.
flow.say: When I was your age, these people looked after me. Is that more or fewer than yours?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up who looked after them as a child. Compare with your count.
flow.context: In this step of Many Hands you compare your carers with a grown-up's.

ask.q: Why might a human child need more carers than a calf does?
good: We take many years to grow up.
There is a lot to learn.
A parent may have another baby before the first child can manage alone.

flow.think: An elephant calf also has aunts and older sisters. What do elephants and people have in common that might explain it?

projects.title: Two on One Nest: a pigeon nest diary (if pigeons nest near you)
projects.context: In this four-day project you watch one pigeon nest for ten minutes a day. You find out whether two different birds sit on it, and when they change over. Pigeons nest on ledges, lofts and air conditioner units in most Indian towns.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a timer or a clock
binoculars, if you have them

projects.safety: Watch from inside, through a window or grill. Do not touch the nest, the eggs or the chicks, and do not move anything near them. Pigeon droppings can carry germs, so wash your hands after touching the ledge.

schedule.what: Find a nest. Watch for ten minutes. Draw the bird who is sitting, with every mark you can see.
Watch at a different time of day. Is it the same bird? Write the time of any changeover.
Watch at a third time of day. Note who sits, who arrives and what they do when they meet.
Watch once more. Then write one claim, your evidence and your reasoning.

projects.record: Each day write the date, the time, which bird was sitting and anything the two birds did together. On day 4 write what I think, what I saw, and why.

setup.art: A pigeon sitting on a nest of twigs behind an air conditioner unit on a building ledge, seen through a window grill.
setup.caption: 1. Find a pigeon nest you can see from inside. Do not go close.

setup.art: A notebook page with two pigeon outlines labelled 'Bird 1' and 'Bird 2', with notes on wing bars, neck colour and one white feather.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each bird's marks so that you can tell the two apart.

setup.art: Two pigeons at a nest, one stepping off the eggs and one stepping on, with a clock showing the time.
setup.caption: 3. Watch at different times of day. Write when they change over.

flow.do: Find a nest with a sitting bird. Watch for ten minutes from inside. Your child draws the bird's marks, takes a photo, or says them aloud. Look for marks such as the wing bars, the neck colour, white feathers or a damaged toe.
flow.say: Who is on the nest? Draw every mark you can see, or tell me what they are. We need to know this bird again tomorrow.
flow.kid: Find a nest. Watch for ten minutes. Draw the bird's marks. Or take a photo. Or tell them to your grown-up.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Two on One Nest. You find a nest and draw the bird who is sitting.
flow.parent: Pigeons breed in most months of the year in Indian towns. If you find no nest, watch any pair of pigeons, crows or mynas on a ledge instead. Note what the two do together, and whether both carry twigs or food.

flow.do: On days 2 and 3, watch for ten minutes at a different time of day from day 1. Your child decides whether the sitting bird is the same one, and writes the evidence. If a second bird comes, note the time and what the two do.
flow.say: Is this the same bird as before? How do you know? Watch for the other one arriving. Write the time if they swap.
flow.kid: Watch at a new time each day. Is it the same bird? Write how you know.
flow.context: These are days 2 and 3 of Two on One Nest. You look for a second bird and a changeover.
flow.wait: Do this once a day for two days
flow.parent: Male and female pigeons look almost alike, so your child may be unsure, and should say so. 'I could not tell' is an honest result. Early morning, midday and late afternoon are good times to compare.

flow.do: On day 4, watch once more. Then your child writes one claim, the evidence for it and the reasoning. Ask what they would need to be surer.
flow.say: What do you think now? Do two birds share this nest? What did you see that tells you? What would make you surer?
flow.kid: Watch once more. Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.context: This is day 4 of Two on One Nest. You say what four days of watching showed.

ask.q: How sure are you that two different birds sat on the nest? What would make you surer?
good: I saw them change over, so I am sure.
I think the marks were different, but I am not certain.
A photo each day would help.
Watching for a whole day would help.

flow.think: Scientists could not tell which chicks had which father until they could test DNA. What can watching show, and what can it not show?

challenges.title: The Parent Is Away: build a nest that keeps an egg warm alone
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a nest from things at home. It must keep a tumbler of warm water warm for 15 minutes with nobody 'sitting'. A bird who raises eggs alone has the same problem every time she or he leaves to feed.
challenges.problem: A parent who sits alone must leave the eggs to find food. Build a nest that keeps a small tumbler of warm water as warm as possible for 15 minutes while the parent is away. Test it against a bare tumbler.
constraints: Use only things already at home, such as newspaper, cloth scraps, cotton wool, a cardboard box, dry leaves or coconut fibre.
Nothing may heat the tumbler. No hot water bottle, no sunlight and no stove.
The parent must be able to get back in. The top must open in five seconds or less.
The nest must fit on a dinner plate, and you have ten minutes to build it.

materials.item: small steel tumblers of the same size
warm water, about as warm as a nice bath
newspaper, cloth scraps, cotton wool, a small cardboard box and any dry leaves or coconut fibre
a dinner plate and a timer
a thermometer, if you have one

general: Wrap the tumbler in several layers of cloth or newspaper.
Stand it inside a box packed with crumpled paper.
Cover the top, because a lot of warmth leaves with the damp air that rises from the water.
creative: Line the nest with something fluffy that traps still air, as an eider duck lines her nest with her own down feathers.
Lift the tumbler off the cold floor on a thick pad, as a penguin father keeps the egg on his feet.
Bury the tumbler in a deep heap. The Nicobar megapode, a bird of the Nicobar Islands, buries eggs in a mound and lets the mound keep them warm.
Make the nest small and snug. A big empty space inside lets the air move and carry warmth away.
challenges.your_turn: Now design a nest for the opposite problem. Some birds lay their eggs on hot open sand, where the eggs could cook. Build or sketch a nest, or tell a thing the parent could do, that keeps an egg cool for 15 minutes.

setup.art: A heap of home materials on a table: newspaper, cloth scraps, cotton wool, a small cardboard box, and a dinner plate to build on.
setup.caption: 1. Gather materials from home. The nest must fit on a dinner plate.

setup.art: A child packing crumpled newspaper around an empty steel tumbler inside a small box, with a cloth flap for a lid.
setup.caption: 2. Build the nest around an empty tumbler. Make a top that opens fast.

setup.art: Two tumblers of water side by side, one inside the home-made nest and one bare on the table, with a timer showing 15 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Fill both tumblers with warm water. Leave them for 15 minutes, then compare.

flow.do: Read the problem and the constraints aloud. Ask your child where the warmth of a tumbler goes, and what could slow it down. They sketch a plan.
flow.say: A warm tumbler cools down. What could slow that? Tell me your plan, or sketch your nest, before you build.
flow.kid: Make a plan for your nest. Sketch it, or tell it to your grown-up.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Parent Is Away. You think about where warmth escapes and plan a nest.

ask.q: Where does the warmth of the tumbler go?
good: Up into the air from the top of the water.
Into the table through the bottom.
Out through the steel sides.

flow.do: Your child builds the nest around an empty tumbler in ten minutes. Check that it fits on the plate and that the top opens in five seconds.
flow.say: You have ten minutes. Build it around the empty tumbler. Show me that the top opens quickly.
flow.kid: Build your nest in ten minutes. Check that it fits the plate. Check that the top opens fast.
flow.context: In this step of The Parent Is Away you build the nest.
flow.parent: Let your child make their own choices, even ones you expect to fail. The test will show what works.

flow.do: Mix warm water and fill both tumblers to the same level. Put one in the nest and close the top. Leave the other bare beside it. Measure or feel both. Start a 15-minute timer.
flow.say: I will pour the water. You put one tumbler in the nest and close it. The bare one is for comparing. Start the timer.
flow.kid: Put one tumbler in the nest. Leave one bare. Start the timer.
flow.context: In this step of The Parent Is Away you start the test against a bare tumbler.
flow.parent: The water should be warm and never hot. While you wait, your child can start the 'your turn' drawing.

flow.do: After 15 minutes, open the nest. Compare the two tumblers with a thermometer, or with one finger in each and eyes shut. Your child says what worked, changes one thing and says what they expect it to do.
flow.say: Open it. Which is warmer, and by how much? What part of your nest did the most? Change one thing and tell me what you expect.
flow.kid: Compare the two tumblers. Then change one thing about your nest and say why.
flow.context: In this step of The Parent Is Away you test the nest and improve it.

ask.q: Which part of your nest did the most to keep the warmth in?
good: The cover on top.
The thick paper all around.
Lifting it off the floor.

flow.parent: If the two tumblers feel the same, the nest is probably open at the top or thin underneath. A good nest keeps the water clearly warmer than the bare tumbler after 15 minutes.

items.p: What makes an animal female?
opts: She makes the larger sex cells
She is smaller than the male
items.why: A female is the one who makes egg cells, the larger sex cells. Caring and size do not decide it. Jacana females are bigger than males and do not sit on the eggs.

items.p: A seahorse father carries the young. Why is he still called male?
opts: He does not feed the young
items.why: Male means the maker of the smaller sex cells, the sperm. Carrying the young does not change which sex cells he makes.

items.p: In most kinds of birds, both parents care for the young.
items.why: True. Both parents care in about four out of five kinds of birds. Eggs need warmth almost all the time, and either parent can give it.

items.p: In most kinds of mammals, the father helps to raise the young.
items.why: False. Fathers help in about one kind of mammal in ten, or fewer. The young grow inside the mother and then need her milk.

items.p: A female who leads her group, such as an old elephant, is called a ____.
items.why: A matriarch is a female leader. In elephants she is usually the oldest female in the family.

items.p: Match each family system to an animal that lives that way.
items.why: Sarus cranes live as pairs. A silverback gorilla lives with several females. A female jacana has several mates. Elephant aunts and sisters help with calves.

items.p: Sort each animal by who looks after the eggs or young.
items.why: A seal pup needs only milk. A king cobra mother guards her nest. Jacana and water bug fathers carry or sit alone. Pigeons and hornbills need two parents.

items.p: In the Warm Egg Test, which tumbler lost the least warmth?
opts: The one covered half the time
items.why: A cover slows the loss of warmth. The tumbler that was never bare lost the least. If you chose the half-covered one, remember that it lost warmth in every bare minute.

items.p: What are the two parts of sexual selection?
opts: Competing for partners and choosing partners
Finding food and hiding from hunters
items.why: Sexual selection is about winning partners, by competing with rivals and by being chosen. Finding food and hiding are about staying alive, which is a different matter.

items.p: A guard kept 12, 11 and 12 coins in three tries. What is the middle number?
items.why: Put the numbers in order: 11, 12, 12. The middle one is 12. The middle number is not pulled about by one odd try.

items.p: Why can a pigeon father help with the eggs, when a bull cannot help much with a calf?
items.a: Eggs need warmth, and a father can sit on them as well as a mother can. A calf grows inside the mother and then needs milk, which only she makes.
items.why: A strong answer names what the young need in each case, and says who is able to give it.

items.p: Name two things a seahorse father's pouch does for the young inside.
items.a: Any two of these. It brings them oxygen. It gives them some food. It carries away their waste. It keeps them safe from being eaten.
items.why: The pouch does much of what a mammal mother's body does for a baby before birth.

items.p: Draw a jacana family on a pond: one female and her mates. Label who sits on the eggs.
items.a: A larger bird walking on the leaves, and two to four smaller birds each sitting on a nest. The smaller birds are labelled as the males who sit on the eggs.
items.why: A strong drawing makes the female larger, shows her off the nests, and labels the males as the sitters.

items.p: Why does an elephant family do better with an old leader?
opts: She remembers friends, strangers and places
items.why: In tests, families with older leaders told friends from strangers better. Her memory is what helps the family. Strength was not what the scientists found.

items.p: A jacana mother lays her eggs and leaves them with the father.

views.says: She is a bad mother. A mother should stay with her eggs.
The chicks are looked after. 'Bad' is a word about people's duties, and she is a jacana.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Give your reason.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer notices that the chicks are cared for by the father, and asks whether a word for human duties fits a bird.
items.why: Both views agree on what the jacana does. They differ on whether a human judgement can be put on it.

items.p: Ten female and ten male seals have ten pups. One male fathers eight. How many do the other nine males share?
items.why: Every pup has one father. If one male fathered 8 of the 10, only 2 are left for the other nine males. Most of them fathered none.

items.p: Why is the sex that spends more on each young usually the choosier one?
opts: A poor choice costs them more
items.why: A cow who chooses badly loses a whole year. A bull loses almost nothing. Choosiness follows the cost. In jacanas the father spends more, and he is the one the females compete for.

items.p: All the females in a group together have the same number of young as all the males together.
items.why: True. Each young has exactly one mother and one father, so the two totals must be equal. What differs is how evenly the young are shared out.

items.p: Two birds who share a nest are always the only parents of the chicks in it.
items.why: False. DNA tests found chicks with an outside father in about nine out of ten kinds of birds tested. Living together and being the parents are separate questions.

items.p: A family system with one female and several males is called ____.
items.why: Polyandry means one female with several male partners. Jacanas live this way.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: several partners each, no lasting pair
items.why: The names describe who pairs with whom. They are not grades from good to bad.

items.p: Put in order what happens when seahorses breed.
a: The pair greet each other each morning
The female passes her eggs into the male's pouch
The eggs are fertilised inside the pouch
The pouch brings oxygen and food to the young
The father pushes out the live young
items.why: The mother makes the eggs, and the father does the carrying and gives birth.

items.p: In one kind of animal, males are five times as heavy as females. Which family is most likely?
items.why: Males become much heavier where a few males win most partners by fighting, as in elephant seals. In pairs, the sexes are usually close in size.

items.p: A male Mormon cricket gives the female a big packet of food. What did scientists find?
items.why: The male spends a lot on each mating, so he becomes the choosy one. This is the role swap that Trivers's idea predicts.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Jacana. Seahorse. Giant water bug. Elephant seal.
items.a: Elephant seal. In elephant seals the mother alone cares for the young. In the other three, the father does.
items.why: Jacana fathers sit on the eggs, seahorse fathers carry them in a pouch, and water bug fathers carry them on their backs.

items.p: Tumbler A fell from 41 to 39 degrees. Tumbler C fell from 41 to 35. How many more degrees did C lose?
items.why: A lost 2 degrees and C lost 6. 6 take away 2 is 4. The bare tumbler lost three times as much as the covered one.

items.p: A fish father already guards a patch of sea floor. Explain why guarding eggs there costs him little extra.
items.a: He is already there, driving rivals away from the patch. The eggs lie on the same patch, so guarding them needs almost no extra time or energy. He can also guard the eggs of several females at once.
items.why: A strong answer says that the guarding was already being done for another reason.

items.p: Hyena females lead, and jacana females fight. What does this show about the claim 'in nature, males lead'?
items.a: The claim is not true of all animals. It was drawn from a few well-known animals, such as gorillas. Other animals do the reverse, and many have no leader.
items.why: A strong answer says that a few examples cannot make a rule, and gives at least one animal that does not fit.

items.p: Draw an egg cell and a sperm side by side. Label which is larger and what each one carries.
items.a: A large round egg cell labelled 'half the instructions, plus food'. A much smaller sperm with a tail, labelled 'half the instructions, almost no food'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a big difference in size, and shows that both carry half of the instructions.

items.p: Do the sex cells decide who cares for the young?

views.says: Mostly, yes. Across many animals, females care more and males compete more.
No. Care goes to whoever gains most by giving it. Look at jacanas and seahorses.

items.ask: Which view fits the evidence in this lesson better? What would you want to count to find out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and names something to count, such as how many kinds of animals fit each pattern.
items.why: Both views accept the same facts. They differ on whether the exceptions are rare or whether surroundings decide most of it. Scientists still argue about this.

items.p: Some pond algae make sex cells of one size only. What follows from that?
opts: They have no females and no males
items.why: Female and male are defined by two sizes of sex cell. With one size there are no two sexes, yet the cells still join and make young.

items.p: Why might middle-sized sex cells do badly?
opts: Too few to find partners, too small to feed young
They swim too fast to join
items.why: Tiny cells win by being many. Large cells win by feeding the young well. A middle size gets neither gain. This is the leading idea, and it is not proved.

items.p: The sand on a turtle beach gets warmer every year. What is likely to change?
items.why: In sea turtles the warmth of the nest sets the sex of the hatchling. Warmer nests give more females. Too few males could become a problem.

items.p: A clownfish can be a father one year and a mother in a later year.
items.why: True. All clownfish start as males. If the female of a group is lost, her mate changes into a female.

items.p: What a parent has already spent on a young is a good reason to keep spending.
items.why: False. What is spent cannot be got back. What matters is what the parent would gain or lose from now on. Trivers made this mistake in 1972, and others corrected it.

items.p: An animal who makes both egg cells and sperm is called a ____.
items.why: Earthworms and garden snails are hermaphrodites. Each one is both female and male.

items.p: Sort each one: can you find it out by watching, or does it need a DNA test?
items: the male sits on the eggs
the big bird chased an intruder
items.why: Watching shows who lives with whom and who does what. Only a DNA test shows who the parents are.

items.p: Put these in order, from males much heavier to females heavier.
items.why: A male elephant seal is about five times as heavy as a female. A female bronze-winged jacana is much heavier than a male. The order follows who competes for partners.

items.p: A female jacana lays 4 eggs for each of her 3 mates. How many eggs is that?
items.why: 4 times 3 is 12. She can lay so many because she does not sit on any of them.

items.p: A new bird is found. The females are bigger and brighter than the males. Predict who sits on the eggs, and explain.
items.a: Probably the males. When females are the bigger, brighter sex, they are usually the ones competing for partners. That happens when males do most of the caring, as in jacanas.
items.why: A strong answer uses the link between who spends more on the young and who competes, and says 'probably', because it is a tendency.

items.p: 'Some animals keep harems, so people should too.' Explain what is wrong with this reasoning.
items.a: Other animals live in every kind of family, so you could pick an animal to support any rule. What happens in nature is a fact. It cannot tell people what is fair or right.
items.why: A strong answer says that a fact about what happens is not a rule about what ought to happen, and notes that other animals do the opposite.

items.p: In the One Guard Test the coins could not move or choose. Name one way real female seals differ from coins.
items.a: Real females move about and choose. Many female elephant seals also mate with males away from the harem.
items.why: A strong answer sees the limit of the model: the guarded ones are living beings who act for themselves.

items.p: Draw two beaches: one where a male seal could keep a harem, and one where he could not. Label why.
items.a: One small beach with the females crowded together and one male beside them, labelled 'close, so he can guard them'. One long beach with the females far apart, labelled 'spread out, so he cannot'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that what matters is how closely the females gather.

items.p: A famous fruit fly test was repeated in 2012, and the result did not hold. What does that teach?
opts: Even famous results must be checked again
items.why: A result is trusted more when others can repeat it. One test, however famous, is a start. Most old results do hold when they are repeated, so the second answer goes too far.

items.p: Seahorse fathers carry the young. Why did the carrying fall to fathers?

views.says: The father carries while the mother makes the next eggs. The pair has more young that way.
The eggs are fertilised in his own pouch, so he is sure the young are his.

items.ask: Which idea seems stronger to you? What could scientists compare to test it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks one with a reason, and suggests a comparison, such as pipefish with and without closed pouches, or how quickly pairs produce the next batch.
items.why: Nobody knows the answer yet. Both ideas may be partly right.

quiz.p: Among all animals, which one is the female?
opts: The one who makes egg cells
The one who sits on the eggs
quiz.why: Female means the maker of the larger sex cells, the egg cells. If you chose 'sits on the eggs', remember the jacana father and the emperor penguin father.

quiz.p: Peahens pick among peacocks. Blackbuck males fight each other. Both are parts of what?
quiz.why: Choosing and competing are the two parts of sexual selection. Parental care is what happens after the eggs or young arrive.

quiz.p: Every pup has one mother and one father, so female and male seals have the same total number of pups.
quiz.why: True. The totals must match. But the pups are shared evenly among the mothers and very unevenly among the fathers.

quiz.p: One female jacana has three mates. What is this family system called?
quiz.why: Polyandry is one female with several males. Polygyny is the reverse, one male with several females.

quiz.p: One male gorilla lives with several females. What is this family system called?
quiz.why: Polygyny is one male with several females. In promiscuity, both sexes have several partners and no group stays around one male.

quiz.p: In jacanas the father does all the caring. Who competes for partners?
quiz.why: The sex that spends less on each young competes for the sex that spends more. In jacanas the fathers spend more, so the females compete.

quiz.p: In the Warm Egg Test, what did the lid and cloth do?
opts: They slowed the loss of warmth
quiz.why: A cover only slows the loss. The warmth that left in the bare minutes did not come back. If you chose 'made new warmth', remember that even tumbler A cooled a little.

quiz.p: Why do fathers help with the young in so few kinds of mammals?
opts: Only mothers carry the baby and make milk
quiz.why: What the young need most, a warm body to grow in and then milk, only the mother can give. So in most mammals a father can add little.

quiz.p: Where do young seahorses grow before they are born?
opts: In a pouch on the father
quiz.why: The mother puts her eggs into the father's brood pouch. He carries them for 9 to 45 days and then gives birth.

quiz.p: A spotted hyena clan is usually led by a female.
quiz.why: True. Hyena females outrank the males, and a cub takes the rank just below their mother.

quiz.p: In tests, what did elephant families with older leaders do better?
quiz.why: Families with older matriarchs bunched together at a stranger's call and stayed calm at a friend's. The leader's memory helped everyone.

quiz.p: Some animals keep harems. Does that show how people should live?
opts: No. A fact is not a rule
Yes, if the animal is a mammal
quiz.why: Other animals live in every kind of family. What happens in nature is a fact about them. It cannot tell people what is fair or right.

applications: People who protect sea turtle nests measure how warm the sand is, because the warmth decides how many hatchlings are female and how many are male.
Zoos that breed rare animals now often let the animals choose their own partners, because pairs who choose each other tend to have more young.
People who protect elephants try hardest to keep the old females safe, because a family that loses the matriarch loses what she remembers.
Scientists use DNA tests to find out which animals are the parents of which young, in wild birds and in breeding programmes for rare animals.
Poultry farms hatch eggs in incubators that hold a steady warmth and turn the eggs, doing the work of a sitting hen.
In Arunachal Pradesh, a nest adoption programme pays local people to guard hornbill nest trees, so that sealed-in mothers and chicks stay safe.

open_questions.q: Why did carrying the young fall to the father in seahorses?
open_questions.why_open: There are several ideas, about speed, about being sure of being the father, and about small steps from guarding. Nobody has found a test that settles it.

open_questions.q: Why do so many living beings mix their instructions with a partner at all, instead of simply copying themselves?
open_questions.why_open: Copying yourself is quicker, and some lizards, insects and plants do it. Scientists think mixing helps the young to resist germs and to cope with change, but they still argue about which reason matters most.

open_questions.q: Why do females lead among spotted hyenas?
open_questions.why_open: Hyena females are only slightly larger than males. Ideas include help from relatives, and the way cubs take their mother's rank. Scientists have not agreed.

open_questions.q: How did two sizes of sex cell first arise?
open_questions.why_open: The maths of 1972 shows that it could have happened through many small cells finding more partners. It happened too long ago to watch, and other causes may have played a part.

open_questions.q: As beaches warm, will sea turtles change where or when they nest, so that some males still hatch?
open_questions.why_open: Turtles have lived through warm and cool ages before. Nobody knows whether they can change quickly enough this time.

ask_kids: Who did something for you today before you asked? Did they give something up to do it?
Look at the pigeons on that ledge. Can you tell which two are a pair? What makes you think so?
If you were a bird sitting on eggs, how would you get your food?
Is that something you saw, or something you guessed?
Why do you think the male deer has antlers and the female has none?
Who in our family remembers the most? What do they know that nobody else does?
A turtle never meets her young. A human child is looked after for years. What is different about what the young need?
If you could not tell a mother bird from a father bird by looking, how could you find out?

jokes.j: Why do pigeon parents never argue about whose turn it is?

jokes.a: He already had something on his feet.

jokes.a: 'Good luck. The sea is that way.'

jokes.a: 'I packed all the lunch. What did you bring?'

jokes.j: Why is a male elephant seal bad at sharing?
jokes.a: He thinks the whole beach is his.

maths.problem: In Kavya's Warm Egg Test, all three tumblers started at 41 degrees. After 20 minutes, A was at 39, B was at 37.5 and C was at 35. How many degrees did each lose? B was covered for half the time. Did B lose exactly halfway between A and C?
maths.answer: A lost 2 degrees, B lost 3.5 and C lost 6. Halfway between 2 and 6 is 4. B lost 3.5, so B ended a little nearer to A than to C.
maths.explain: 41 take away 39 is 2. 41 take away 37.5 is 3.5. 41 take away 35 is 6. To find halfway between 2 and 6, add them and halve: 8 divided by 2 is 4. B lost half a degree less than that. Your own result may fall on the other side of halfway, and that is fine.
maths.context: In the Warm Egg Test, tumbler A is always covered, B is covered for half the time and C is never covered.
maths.why_maths: The question was whether half the cover gives half the protection. Only by finding the halfway point can you answer it.

maths.problem: A beach has 10 female and 10 male elephant seals. 10 pups are born, one to each female. One huge male is the father of 8 of them. What is the average number of pups for a female? For a male? What is the largest number of the other nine males who can have fathered a pup?
maths.answer: The average is 1 pup for a female and 1 pup for a male. Only 2 pups are left for the other nine males, so at most 2 of them are fathers. At least 7 males have no pups.
maths.explain: 10 pups shared among 10 females is 1 each. Every pup also has one father, so 10 pups shared among 10 males is also 1 each on average. But 10 take away 8 leaves 2 pups for nine males. The average is the same for both sexes. How evenly the pups are shared is very different.
maths.context: In Size Detective, you found that a male elephant seal is about five times as heavy as a female. This problem shows what the males are fighting over.
maths.why_maths: People often say that males have more young than females. Counting shows that the totals must be equal, and that the real difference is in the sharing.

maths.problem: A pheasant-tailed jacana father sits on a clutch for about 27 days. The breeding season lasts about 120 days. Even if he took a new clutch the day the last one hatched, how many clutches could he hatch? A female can lay up to 10 clutches in a season. What does she need?
maths.answer: He could hatch 4 clutches at the very most. She can lay 10, so she needs several mates. There are not enough free fathers, so the females compete for them.
maths.explain: 120 divided by 27 is 4, with 12 days left over, which is not enough for a fifth clutch. In real life he also looks after the chicks, so he manages fewer than 4. The female can lay clutches faster than any one male can raise them. Males who are free to sit are the scarce thing, and the scarce sex is the one competed for.
maths.context: In Who Looks After the Young, you found that a jacana father raises the chicks alone while the mother lays more eggs.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the season by the sitting time shows why jacana females fight over males. No amount of watching shows that as clearly as the numbers do.

maths.problem: A female bronze-winged jacana weighs about 280 grams and a male about 175 grams. A male elephant seal weighs about 3,300 kilograms and a female about 600. In each animal, how many times as heavy is the heavier sex? Which difference is bigger?
maths.answer: The female jacana is 1.6 times as heavy as the male. The male seal is 5.5 times as heavy as the female. The seal's difference is much bigger, and it runs the other way.
maths.explain: 280 divided by 175 is 1.6. 3,300 divided by 600 is 5.5. You cannot compare grams with kilograms directly, but you can compare the two 'times as heavy' numbers. In both animals the heavier sex is the one that fights for partners.
maths.context: In Size Detective, you divided the male's weight by the female's weight for seven animals.
maths.why_maths: A jacana and a seal are far too different in size to compare by weight. 'How many times as heavy' lets you compare them fairly.

maths.problem: An emperor penguin father may weigh 38 kilograms when winter starts and 18 kilograms about 120 days later. How many kilograms has he lost? Is that more or less than half of his starting weight? About how many grams is that each day?
maths.answer: He has lost 20 kilograms. Half of 38 is 19, so he has lost a little more than half of his weight. That is about 167 grams each day.
maths.explain: 38 take away 18 is 20. Half of 38 is 19, and 20 is more than 19. 20 kilograms is 20,000 grams. 20,000 divided by 120 is about 167. That is roughly the weight of a medium-sized tomato or two idlis, every day for four months, with nothing eaten.
maths.context: In the game Stay or Go, the emperor penguin card says the father holds the egg through the winter without eating.
maths.why_maths: Care is paid for in energy from the parent's body. Working out the daily loss turns 'a lot' into something you can picture.

maths.problem: In Meenakshi's One Guard Test, the guard kept these coins out of 12. Close layout: 12, 12, 11. Spread layout: 9, 10, 4. Far layout: 5, 6, 4. Find the middle number for each layout. Which single try looks odd? Should she leave it out?
maths.answer: The middle numbers are 12, 9 and 5. The try of 4 in the spread layout looks odd. She should keep it in the table and write a note about it. Using the middle number already stops one odd try from changing the result.
maths.explain: In order, the close tries are 11, 12, 12, so the middle is 12. The spread tries are 4, 9, 10, so the middle is 9. The far tries are 4, 5, 6, so the middle is 5. The 4 in the spread layout is far from 9 and 10. Perhaps the guard was tired or looked away. Scientists do not hide a result that does not fit. They record it and say what may have happened.
maths.context: In the One Guard Test, one person guards 12 coins with one hand for 30 seconds, in three layouts, three tries each.
maths.why_maths: Three tries give three different numbers. The middle one gives a fair single number for each layout, even when one try goes wrong.

maths.problem: On the jacana card in Stay or Go, the young get 3 points if one or both parents stay, and 0 if nobody stays. The mother's bonus for going is 3 and the father's is 0. If the father stays, what does the mother score for staying, and for going? If the mother goes, what does the father score for staying, and for going?
maths.answer: If the father stays, the mother scores 3 for staying and 6 for going, so she does better to go. If the mother goes, the father scores 3 for staying and 0 for going, so he does better to stay.
maths.explain: Mother stays: 3 young points. Mother goes while father stays: 3 young points plus her bonus of 3 makes 6. Father stays alone: 3 young points. Father goes too: nobody stays, so 0 young points plus his bonus of 0 makes 0. Each parent's best choice depends on what the other does.
maths.context: In the game Stay or Go, two players are the mother and father of the same young, and each chooses to stay or to go.
maths.why_maths: Working through 'if he stays, then she…' step by step shows why the real jacana family ends up with the father sitting. Nobody has to plan it.

how_we_found_out.context: This is the true story of how one test on fruit flies became a rule for all animals, and how the rule was shown to be wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1948 Angus Bateman put fruit flies together in bottles and counted their young. He reported that males had more young when they had more partners, and that females did not. For about forty years this one test was taken as a rule for all animals. Males were said to be eager, and females coy and faithful. The evidence did not hold. In the 1970s Sarah Blaffer Hrdy watched langur monkeys at Mount Abu in Rajasthan. She reported that the females mated with more than one male. From the late 1980s, DNA tests on birds showed that chicks in one nest often had different fathers. Then, in 2012, Patricia Gowaty's team repeated Bateman's test as closely as they could. They found a flaw. Bateman had told the parents apart by marks that the young flies inherited. Some combinations of those marks killed the young before they could be counted. So his counts of who had mated were wrong. The repeat showed no such difference between the sexes. Scientists still argue about how different the sexes are on average, but the old rule is gone.
how_we_found_out.who: Angus Bateman in England, Sarah Blaffer Hrdy at Mount Abu in India, and Patricia Gowaty with Yong-Kyu Kim and Wyatt Anderson in the United States
how_we_found_out.when: Bateman published in 1948. Hrdy's book The Langurs of Abu came out in 1977. Gowaty's team published their repeat in 2012.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That males of all animals are eager and gain from many partners, while females are coy and gain nothing from more than one. Field studies, DNA tests on chicks and a careful repeat of the first test all showed that this was not a rule.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist holding a glass bottle of fruit flies up to a window, with an old journal page from 1948 open on the bench beside her.

playtest: Every activity was walked through step by step as a parent and child in a city flat would do it. None has yet been tried at home. The Warm Egg Test needs three steel tumblers of one size, two lids, two cloths and warm bath water at about 40 degrees. The differences after 20 minutes are expected to be a few degrees, which a thermometer shows clearly and a finger can usually tell. In a very warm room they may be too small, and the last step says what to do then. Where tumbler B ends between A and C will differ from home to home, and the unit treats any result as fair. A fever thermometer works only between about 32 and 42 degrees. The One Guard Test needs two people, 12 coins and a clear floor, and it only works if the taker tries equally hard every time. Keep taps gentle. Stay or Go has 8 cards, all written out, and needs two players and two coins. Each card was worked through by hand to check that the best choices match what the real animals do. Size Detective needs a calculator. Its weights are typical figures from single studies. The pigeon nest project depends on finding a nest, and gives another way to do it if you cannot. The facts and figures were checked online in November 2026 against encyclopedia articles, journal abstracts and university pages, and the three videos were confirmed on YouTube by title and channel, but their lengths were not. A person should check these before publishing: the weights used for the sarus crane (measured in Australia) and the pheasant-tailed jacana (measured in Thailand), the reason for the jacana family system, which is now written as an idea because nest losses have not been measured well, and the Nicobar megapode and eider duck examples in the nest challenge, which were not looked up again.
